lessons.text:
Heaven never
takes a day off.
lessons.why: The Image: heaven moves with inexhaustible vigor, and the realized person strengthens without ceasing. (Not a line lesson: 1-2-3 would be three line lessons in a row. The critic's 'Heaven never stops.' is 19 characters.)
lessons.feedback: Checked against the Image: 'Heaven moves with inexhaustible vigor. The realized person accordingly strengthens without ceasing.' The idiom is plain and a little funny, it fits HEAVEN over HEAVEN, and it adds persistence to a short whose copy only says 'begin'. Line lengths are 12 and 16 characters. It is not a 9 because it leaves out the second half of the Image: heaven doesn't stop, so the person doesn't either. The picture carries that only if the viewer makes the link. Keep it.

lessons.text:
Frost underfoot:
ice is coming.
lessons.why: Line 1: small signs now tell you what is coming later.
lessons.feedback: Line 1 says 'Treading on frost. Solid ice is coming.' Concrete, a little ominous, and a real surprise next to a short about following well. It adds to the short. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
Without a guide,
let the deer go.
lessons.why: Line 3: chasing deer into the forest without a forester goes wrong, so let it go.
lessons.feedback: Line 3: chasing deer with no forester, 'better to let it go.' 'Guide' for forester is a fair plain word. It is concrete and fits 'boring beats bold' without repeating it. Good.

lessons.text:
Teachers don't
chase students.
lessons.why: The Judgment: it is not I who seek the youth, the youth seeks me. (Not the suggested line 2: 3, 4 and 5 would be three line lessons in a row.)
lessons.feedback: The Judgment says: 'It is not I who seek the inexperienced youth, the inexperienced youth seeks me.' The synthesis has almost the same words ('The teacher doesn't chase the student'). It is plain, concrete and easy to share. The short's copy uses the other half of the Judgment ('ask once / asking twice is shopping'), so this adds the half that comes before it without repeating it. The one weakness is that the Judgment page is the same source the meaning lines already came from, so it is less of a surprise than a line lesson. Line 5, where the clueless youth is the one who does well, would be more surprising, but the kind-variety rule blocks a line lesson here. Keep it.

lessons.text:
Uninvited guests?
Receive them well.
lessons.why: Line 6: three uninvited guests arrive; treat them with respect and it ends well.
lessons.feedback: Line 6: three uninvited guests, receive them with respect, it ends well. Concrete, a little funny, and a good twist on 'wait well'. Consider 'Three strangers show up?' to keep the book's specific number, but it works as is.

lessons.text:
Won the belt,
lost it by noon.
lessons.why: Line 6: a win taken by fighting is stripped away before the morning is out.
lessons.feedback: Line 6: 'awarded the champion's belt. By morning's end, stripped of it three times.' 'By noon' is a fair plain version. Concrete and funny. It illustrates 'pushing to the end costs you' without repeating the wording. Could add the 'three times' if it fits, but it is good.

lessons.text:
Unseen water
under the earth.
lessons.why: Accepted: water within the earth is the army, the people held in reserve.
lessons.feedback: Approved standard. It matches the Image and the EARTH over WATER picture.

lessons.text:
Friends at lunch,
holding together.
lessons.why: Accepted: Renoir's crowded table shows holding together at a glance.
lessons.feedback: Approved standard. The painting makes the point at a glance.

lessons.text:
Wheels come off,
the couple glares.
lessons.why: Line 3: the cart throws its spokes and husband and wife glare at each other; when something structural breaks, people on the same side turn on each other.
lessons.feedback: Line 3 says exactly this: the cart throws off its spokes, husband and wife glare at each other. The rules check passes: 6 words, 16 and 18 characters. It is concrete and a little funny, in the same register as the approved 'guest, not an inspector'. It adds something new after the short's 'not yet / work on yourself' copy and fits the lit-line picture. One small option: 'Spokes fly off,' is closer to the text, but 'Wheels come off' reads faster. I would post it.

lessons.text:
The tiger's tail:
it does not bite.
lessons.why: Accepted: tread carefully and even the tiger does not bite.
lessons.feedback: Approved standard: concrete, surprising, true to the Judgment.

lessons.text:
No flat ground
without a slope.
lessons.why: Line 3: no level plain without slopes. Good times tilt, and that is normal.
lessons.feedback:
Almost word for word from line 3 ('No level plain without slopes'). It answers the hook 'Good times, now what?' well, since good times tilt, and it doesn't repeat 'keep it moving' or 'contact, not a vacation'. It is concrete, the kind of thing a person would say, and the book's own image, so it is not an invented metaphor. The viewer needs a moment to get from ground to good times, which keeps it at 8 rather than 9. If you want it quicker, the line's second clause, 'No going
without return.', is an option, but the slope version is the more vivid of the two.

lessons.text:
The great leaves,
the small arrives.
lessons.why: The Judgment's own words, 'The great departs, the small arrives': the viewer can check it against the page on screen, and it says why things stall. (Judgment, not line 5, so 11-12-13 are not three line lessons in a row.)
lessons.feedback:
True to the Judgment ('The great departs, the small arrives') and it passes the checker (17 and 18 chars, 6 words). It fits the Judgment page, and it doesn't repeat the hook ('no one's talking'), meaning ('hold back', 'bad deal') or question ('turn down'). The problem is that it is cryptic in the same way as the rejected watchtower lesson. A viewer who doesn't know the hexagram can't tell whether 'the great' and 'the small' are people, things or amounts, so in two seconds they learn a riddle, not a fact. 'Leaves' against 'arrives' also reads like translation, not talk. Better: say who they are, using the synthesis ('it specifically blocks the people who care'): 'Good people leave,
small ones arrive.' (17/17). Or, closer to the Judgment's first clause: 'Small people in,
good people out.' (16/16). If the kind can change without making 11-12-13 three line lessons, line 5 is the surprising material: the standstill ends and the great person says 'What if it fails?' twice, e.g. 'It ends. Still:
what if it fails?' (15/18). Avoid a 'lines' lesson on Heaven over Earth ('stop talking'), because it would repeat the hook.

lessons.text:
First weeping,
then laughter.
lessons.why: Line 5: fellowship can start in tears and end in laughing together.
lessons.feedback: Line 5: 'first with weeping and wailing, then laughter.' Human, a little surprising, and it adds to 'keep it open' without repeating it. Good.

lessons.text:
A full cart,
a place to go.
lessons.why: Line 2: a great cart for loading and somewhere to go; you have the capacity and the destination.
lessons.feedback: It is true to line 2 (a great cart for loading, somewhere to go), plain, and fits the lit-line picture. The rules check passes (6 words, 12 and 14 characters). The problem is that it lands soft: 'a full cart, a place to go' comes across as a generic good omen, so a new viewer learns little, and it does not connect to the short's 'people see / put things right / what would you fix first?'. Two ways to lift it: make the point sharper and more active, e.g. 'Load the big cart.\nKnow where it goes.' (17/18 chars); or use line 1, which is more surprising at the start of abundance and ties to 'fix first': the book says stay clear of harm, e.g. 'Rich now? Keep\nclear of harm.' The Klimt painting is available, but its own note says it does not carry 'putting things right', so keep it as a line lesson.

lessons.text:
Level the heaps,
fill the holes.
lessons.why: The Image: the mountain within the earth reduces what is excessive and increases what is lacking.
lessons.feedback: True to the Image (reduces what's excessive, increases what's lacking, weighing to distribute evenly). 'Heaps' and 'holes' are a fair concrete rendering and suit the picture of the mountain sunk inside the earth. It is plain and short, and it adds a new idea (redistribution) to a short about credit and finishing quietly. It ends well. I would post it. A minor risk: the link to 'modesty' is left to the picture. Fine as is.

lessons.text:
Shout about it
and it goes wrong.
lessons.why: Line 1: proclaiming your enthusiasm is adverse.
lessons.feedback: Line 1: 'Proclaiming one's enthusiasm. Adverse.' 'Shout about it' is a plain, slightly funny version. It adds a warning to 'give it a shape' without repeating it. Good.

lessons.text:
Grabbed the kid,
lost the adult.
lessons.why: Line 2: attached to the small child, losing the mature one. No verdict, only the trade: following one thing means letting go of another.
lessons.feedback: True: line 2 reads 'Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.' and the synthesis says almost exactly 'You grabbed the kid and lost the adult.' Mechanics pass (16/15 chars, 6 words). It is concrete, a little surprising, and it adds to a short about stopping for the day: following one thing costs you another. What holds it under 8 is 'Grabbed the kid'. Read cold under a lit line, it sounds like a snatching or a custody fight, and the viewer has to work out that it describes a choice. Plainer and closer to the line text: 'Keep the child,\nlose the adult.' (15/15) or 'Hold the little one,' is too long, so use the first. Keep the kind (line).

lessons.text:
Plan three days,
check three days.
lessons.why: The Judgment's 'three days before, three days after' gives the repair a concrete measure: think before and after.
lessons.feedback: The Judgment says 'three days before the new start, three days after'. 'Plan' and 'check' are the synthesis's reading ('deliberate on both sides'), not the text's words. It is concrete and fits the Judgment page. But it overlaps with the copy's 'Rushed repairs don't hold', and 'plan three days, check three days' sounds like a productivity tip. Closer to the page: 'Three days before,\nthree days after.' (17/16). Or try line 1, which is more surprising: 'Fix your father's\nmess: no blame.' (17/14), from 'If there is a son to examine it, no fault falls'.

lessons.text:
Too comfortable?
Worry a little.
lessons.why: Line 3: a comfortable approach supports nothing, but once you worry about it there is no fault.
lessons.feedback: Line 3: 'Comfortable approach. No direction is supported. Once one worries about it: no fault.' The lesson is faithful, plain and a little funny, and it answers the question 'What will you prepare now?' well. It doesn't repeat the copy's spring/autumn idea. Good to post.

lessons.text:
Look like a guest,
not an inspector.
lessons.why: Approved: at line 4 the supported move is to be the sovereign's guest, observing with a visitor's courtesy.
lessons.feedback: Approved standard. True to line 4's synthesis (guest, not inspector). It is concrete and a little funny. It extends the copy's 'go and look' without repeating it.

lessons.text:
Lightning shows,
thunder hits.
lessons.why: Fire over thunder: first see the problem clearly, then bite down with force.
lessons.feedback:
The Image says 'Lightning and thunder', and the synthesis says 'first the clarity, then the force.' So it's true, but as written it only describes weather. The point (see it clearly, then act) is left for the viewer to work out, and 'thunder hits' repeats the copy's 'bite down.' The picture's label says FIRE, not lightning, which is a small mismatch. Say the point in plain words: 'See it clearly,
then bite down.' (15/14). Or use the Image's own instruction: 'Make the rules
clear to all.' Another option is line 4, which is concrete and surprising: 'Bite the bone,
find arrowheads.'

lessons.text:
A white horse?
It's a suitor.
lessons.why: Line 4: the white horse that looks like an attacker is a suitor. Something striking arriving is not always a threat.
lessons.feedback: Glad to post. It is concrete, surprising, a little funny, and quoted almost word for word from line 4 ('This is not an assailant - it is a suitor'). It also adds something to a short about polish versus decisions. One small gap: nothing says the horse looks like a threat, so the twist lands a little softer than it could. Optional version: 'Not a raider.\nA suitor.' Or keep the horse: 'A white horse:\nnot an attack.' The current text is fine.

lessons.text:
The bed breaks at
the legs first.
lessons.why: Collapse starts at the base, the part nobody looks at.
lessons.feedback: True to line 1 ('Splitting the bed at the legs'). 'First' is earned, because lines 2 and 4 go on to the frame and the skin. It is concrete and visual, fits the lit bottom line and backs the copy's 'help those below you' without repeating it. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
Solstice:
kings stayed home.
lessons.why: Thunder within the earth: at the solstice the ancient kings closed the passes and the ruler did not tour the regions.
lessons.feedback: True: the Image says the kings closed the passes at the solstice and the ruler did not tour. It's concrete and a little surprising, and it backs up the short's 'Rest. Only rushing stops it' with a historical fact, not a repeat. Two small problems. The 'Solstice:' opener has the same clipped label-then-colon shape as the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower', and the trigram picture (EARTH over THUNDER) isn't in the words. Plainer: 'At the solstice,\nkings stayed home.' (16/18), or 'Passes shut,\nkings stayed home.' Either would make it an 8.

lessons.text:
Innocent, yet
the ox is taken.
lessons.why: Innocence does not protect you from misfortune; it only means the misfortune is not your fault.
lessons.feedback: True to line 3 (tethered ox taken, innocence meets misfortune). It is concrete and pushes back usefully against the copy's 'stop faking, and it works'. But 'Innocent, yet' is a bit literary, and without 'not your fault' it may not land in two seconds. Plainer: 'Did no wrong,\nstill lost the ox.' (12/16). Line 5 is also strong and surprising: 'Not your illness:\ndon't treat it.' (16/14).

lessons.text:
Cap the calf's
horns early.
lessons.why: Line 4: a board on the young bull's horns, supremely good, is restraint put in place before there is harm.
lessons.feedback: Line 4: 'The young bull's headboard. Supremely resolves well.' The lesson is concrete and a little surprising, and it teaches prevention as a new idea after the copy's 'go public'. 'calf' is a fair plain word for young bull. Good to post.

lessons.text:
Stop staring at
someone's plate.
lessons.why: Line 1 sets down its own spirit tortoise to gape at someone else's meal: envy traded for self-sufficiency.
lessons.feedback: True to line 1 (setting aside your own spirit tortoise to watch another's jaws: adverse). It is concrete and funny, and it adds envy to the copy's 'watch your mouth'. It drops the book's twist that you already had your own food source. If there is room: 'You have your own.\nStop staring.' Fine as is.

lessons.text:
In over your head.
Not your fault.
lessons.why: Line 6, over Hokusai's wave: wading too deep, the water covers the head. Adverse, but no fault.
lessons.feedback: Line 6: 'Wading too deep, the water covers the head. Adverse. No fault.' The synthesis supports reading 'no fault' as 'not your fault' ('It went badly' and 'you were wrong' are separate). With Hokusai's wave it lands at a glance, it's a little funny, and it answers the hook 'Under too much weight?' well. One small thing: the painting entry has no year, and the card needs one (c. 1831).

lessons.text:
Food through
a window: no fault
lessons.why: Line 4: wine and rice handed through the window, and in the end no fault. In the abyss, a small plain offering is enough.
lessons.feedback:
True to line 4 (wine, rice, clay vessels handed through the window; in the end no fault). It's concrete and odd enough to stick, and it answers the short's question 'What's the next small step?' well. But 'no fault' is book jargon a newcomer won't read as anything, and the missing full stop is inconsistent. Drop the verdict and keep the image: 'Rice and wine,
through a window.' (14/17). Or say what it means: 'In the pit, send
food through a window' is too long, so try 'Stuck? Pass food
through a window.' (16/17).

lessons.text:
At sunset, don't
party or wail.
lessons.why: Drumming and singing and lamenting old age are both adverse responses to the setting sun.
lessons.feedback: True to line 3 (drumming and singing vs lamenting old age, adverse). The 'both wrong' reading is the synthesis's, which is fair. It is concrete, a little funny, fits the burnout copy and the lit line. One small change: cite lines[2].synthesis too, since 'don't do either' comes from there.

lessons.text:
This one ends
in a wedding.
lessons.why: The Judgment: taking a wife resolves well. The book cares whether influence becomes a commitment.
lessons.feedback:
It rests on 'Taking a wife resolves well', and it's plain and a little funny. But 'This one ends in a wedding' overstates the text: the book says marrying goes well, not that the story ends in marriage. It also reads like a prediction, close to fortune-telling, and 'this one' has nothing to refer to on the Judgment page. It also has no link to the short's 'make room / already decided'. The famous and surprising part of Influence is the body sequence in the lines. Line 1: 'It starts
in the big toes.' Line 6 (influence in the jaws, cheeks and tongue) against a short about being already decided: 'Last stop:
jaws and tongue.' Or 'Toes first,
tongue last.' (10/11), which a viewer gets at a glance with the lit line. If you keep the Judgment, write 'Taking a wife:
it goes well.' (14/13).

lessons.text:
No game in this
field. Move.
lessons.why: Persistence in the wrong place is wasted: a field with no game.
lessons.feedback: True to line 4 ('A field with no game'). 'Move' is the synthesis's word. It is concrete and funny, and a useful counterweight to 'keep doing'. The break 'this / field.' is a little awkward. 'No game here.\nMove fields.' (13/12) reads cleaner. Glad to post either way. Series note: 8 of these 16 are line (50%, over the 40% target), and 3 are lines.

lessons.text:
Leaving? Take your
people with you.
lessons.why: Line 3: a tangled retreat goes well if you keep your dependents with you instead of cutting them loose.
lessons.feedback:
Line 3 says 'keeping servants and concubines resolves well' and the synthesis says 'bring them along', so the lesson is true to the text. It is concrete and a little surprising. 'Leaving?' repeats the hook ('Time to walk away?'). If you want it sharper: 'Tangled exit? Keep
your people close.' Fine to post as is.

lessons.text:
Ram hits hedge.
Horns get stuck.
lessons.why: Line 3's ram shows that force alone gets power stuck.
lessons.feedback: True to line 3 ('The ram butts the hedge and entangles its horns'). Concrete and a little funny. After the question 'What won't you do with it?' it shows what force alone gets you. The headline clip ('Ram hits hedge') is fine at this length. Ready to post.

lessons.text:
Three audiences
in one day.
lessons.why: The Judgment shows what progress looks like when it comes: horses given in abundance and three audiences with the king in a single day.
lessons.feedback: The Judgment does say this: 'In a single day, granted audience three times.' The problem is the word 'audiences'. A new viewer reads it as a crowd watching, not as meetings with a lord, so the line does not land in two seconds. It also shows only the reward, which the hook ('Finally getting recognized?') already implies. Fix 1, keep the judgment and name who is giving the audience: 'Seen by the lord\nthree times a day.' (16/18). Fix 2, better: use line 4, 'Progressing like a squirrel. Sustained orientation: strained.' It is concrete and a little funny, and it fits the short's 'character first' point: 'Don't get ahead\nlike a squirrel.' Check that the commentary's reading of the squirrel (a greedy, grabbing climber) supports this.

lessons.text:
A prince acted mad
to stay alive.
lessons.why: Line 5: Prince Ji hid his sanity at the tyrant's court, the book's own example of hiding your light to survive.
lessons.feedback:
The line 5 synthesis names Prince Ji, who faked madness at the tyrant's court. A real story gives the meaning ('Keep your light inside') a face, and that is surprising. 'Acted mad' can be read as 'got angry'. 'A prince faked
madness to live.' is less ambiguous.

lessons.text:
Whoever feeds them
holds the family.
lessons.why: Line 2: the one who stays in and feeds everyone is the center of the family, which Chardin's mother at the table shows at a glance.
lessons.feedback:
Line 2 ('attending to the nourishment within', synthesis: 'the person who feeds everyone') plus the Judgment synthesis on holding the center supports it. Chardin's mother serving at the table shows it at a glance, and the lesson moves the short away from rules. 'Holds the family' is a touch abstract. 'Whoever feeds them
is the center.' would be more literal, but this is postable.

lessons.text:
Not an attacker,
a suitor.
lessons.why: Line 6: what looked like a threat was someone coming to propose.
lessons.feedback: True to line 6 ('Not an assailant — a suitor'). Surprising and a little funny, and it adds to 'start small / stay different'. It fits the lit line. It could carry more of the line's picture, e.g. 'A cart of ghosts?\nNo, a suitor.' (16/12 chars), but as written it is ready to post.

lessons.text:
Water stuck
on a mountain.
lessons.why: WATER over MOUNTAIN: water on top of a mountain can't flow and just sits there, the book's picture of obstruction.
lessons.feedback:
The Image says 'Water upon the mountain: obstruction', and the synthesis says 'it can't flow, it just sits there'. The line is plain and matches the WATER over MOUNTAIN picture. But it is closer to a caption than a lesson: it restates the hook 'Hit a wall?' as a picture and teaches nothing new. The line texts are more surprising. Lines 1, 3, 4 and 6 all read 'Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: ...', and line 1 ends in 'praise': 'Going on: stuck.
Coming back: praise.' (16/19; cut to fit, e.g. 'Go on: stuck.
Come back: praise.' 13/17). Line 2, 'It is not a personal matter', would also work: 'Blocked again?
It isn't personal.' (14/18). Either one adds to the 'ask for help' meaning without repeating it.

lessons.text:
Riding with a load
invites thieves.
lessons.why: Line 3: carrying the old burden into freedom makes you a target.
lessons.feedback: True to line 3 ('Carrying a burden while riding in a carriage. Inviting thieves'). Concrete and a little funny, and it goes well with the short's 'let the grudges go', since the old load is the grudge. It is exactly 18 chars on line 1, which is fine. Optional plainer version: 'A load on your back\nin a carriage' is too long, so keep it as is.

lessons.text:
Two small baskets
will do.
lessons.why: The Judgment says two small baskets may be used for the offering: when you have less, a small offering is enough.
lessons.feedback:
The Judgment says 'Two small baskets may be used for the offering.' It is concrete and a little surprising, and it fits the Judgment page. Two problems. First, without the word 'offering' the viewer doesn't know what the baskets are for, so 'will do' only half lands. Second, it partly repeats the meaning line 'give what you can'. Fix 1: 'Two small baskets
are offering enough.' (17/20, too long) or 'A small offering
is enough.' (16/10). Fix 2, better and more surprising: line 3, 'Three people walking lose one person. One person walking finds a companion.' → 'Three walk, lose one.
One walks, finds one.' (needs trimming to 18) or 'Three lose one;
one finds a friend.' (15/18). It is funny, specific, and new next to the short's copy.

lessons.text:
Even bad events
can increase you.
lessons.why: Line 3, the surprising line of Increase: 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.'
lessons.feedback: True to line 3 ('Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.'). It is the surprising line and fits the lit-line picture. It adds a lot beyond 'go now / see good, move toward it', and it ends the short with a twist. It loses points for 'increase you', which is awkward English that no one says out loud. Plainer: 'Even bad events\ncan make you grow.' (17 characters) or 'Bad luck can\nstill help you grow.' With that fix it would be an 8.

lessons.text:
Tell your own
town first.
lessons.why: Before a breakthrough, the Judgment says notify your own city.
lessons.feedback: True to the Judgment ('Notify your own city'). Practical and a little surprising, and it adds to the short's 'say it openly' by saying who to tell first. Plain. Ready to post.

lessons.text:
A lean pig kicks.
Tie it early.
lessons.why: Line 1: the small thing that looks harmless still struggles, so restrain it at the first sign.
lessons.feedback: Line 1 has the tethered lean pig that kicks and struggles and the metal brake, and the synthesis says to check it at the first sign. The lesson is concrete, a little funny, and teaches the hexagram's point, stop the small thing early, in one picture. It adds to 'Charm can be the warning' and doesn't repeat it. Small point: the text says the pig is already tethered and the verb is 'brake', but 'Tie it early' matches the meaning. Post as is.

lessons.text:
One handshake,
laughter again.
lessons.why: Line 1: after confusion, one handclasp restores laughter, so don't worry about the arguments.
lessons.feedback:
True to line 1 ('one handclasp restores laughter. Do not worry'). It answers the hook ('bracing for arguments') warmly and concretely, and ends the short well. Postable. Optional: 'One handshake,
and the laughter's back.' is longer than 18 characters, so keep it as is.

lessons.text:
A tree grows
inside the earth.
lessons.why: EARTH over WIND (wind is also wood): the Image's wood growing within the earth, pushing up through soil before anyone sees it, which answers the hook about slow growth.
lessons.feedback: The Image says 'Within the earth, wood grows'. The line is plain, concrete, and answers the slow-growth hook without repeating 'Small steps, piled up'. The weak point is the picture: the lower trigram will be labelled WIND 風, so the viewer reads EARTH over WIND and then a sentence about a tree. That gap costs the two-second read. The fix is to label it WOOD 木, or WIND/WOOD, for this short. If the label can't change, use line 3, which is strange and memorable: 'Pushing upward into an empty town.' → 'Climbing into\nan empty town.' (13/14) as a line lesson. It is also the same shape as the approved #7 lesson ('Unseen water under the earth'). That is fine alone, but check that the neighbouring hexagrams don't also use lines.

lessons.text:
A lake with
no water.
lessons.why: The two trigrams, LAKE over WATER, show the water drained out below the lake: the empty lake is the book's picture of oppression.
lessons.feedback: The Image says it word for word: 'The lake without water: oppression.' It fits the trigram picture well, LAKE with WATER below it, the water drained out underneath. A new viewer gets a clear picture of what oppression looks like in the book. It gives the source picture behind the short's 'hold your purpose' without repeating it, much like the approved 'Unseen water under the earth.' A little flat. If you want more bite, the Judgment line 'Having words — they are not believed' is concrete, but it is too close to the hook ('Speaking up and nobody listens?'), so keep this one.

lessons.text:
The well is clean.
No one drinks.
lessons.why: Line 3, the only sad line in the book: the well is cleaned and no one drinks, 'my heart's sorrow'.
lessons.feedback: True to line 3 ('The well is cleaned but no one drinks. This is my heart's sorrow'). It is plain, concrete and sad. It turns the hook ('Good things just out of reach?') around, which is surprising. You could post it as is. It sits at the top of the batch with 36.

lessons.text:
Some change only
their faces.
lessons.why: The realized person changes like a leopard; the petty change only their faces, so surface change is not the real thing.
lessons.feedback: True: line 6 says 'The petty change only their faces.' The lesson adds to the short, whose copy is about waiting and trust, and it is a little wry. The problem is that the line sets the petty against the leopard, and the lesson drops the leopard, so it reads as half a sentence. A viewer gets 'some people fake it' but not the point that real change goes deeper. Better to keep the contrast in plain words, e.g. 'Real change goes\npast the face.' Or use line 3, which is concrete and surprising: 'Wait till it's said\nthree times.' That fits 18 characters per line, and the line says trust comes once talk of the change has gone around three times. Check it does not echo the meaning line 'Trust comes on the last day' too closely.

lessons.text:
The legs break.
Duke wears dinner.
lessons.why: The caldron's legs break, the duke's meal spills over him: what happens when the setup isn't right.
lessons.feedback: True to line 4: legs break, the duke's meal overturned, his person soiled. It is concrete and funny, and it pays off the short's 'get set up before you start' by showing what happens when you don't. I would post it. The only flaw is that 'Duke wears dinner' reads like a headline. 'The duke wears\nhis dinner.' is slightly plainer if the line limits allow.

lessons.text:
First fear,
then laughter.
lessons.why: The Judgment puts terror and laughter in sequence: the shock comes, then the laugh.
lessons.feedback: True to the Judgment (terror, terror, then ha, ha) and line 1. Plain, a little funny, and it adds to 'use the fear' without repeating it. It fits the Judgment page. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
Still inside,
while you walk.
lessons.why: The Judgment walks through the courtyard: stillness is not freezing in place, it is keeping still inside while you keep moving.
lessons.feedback: Close to the Judgment synthesis ('You're walking. You just stopped grasping'), but 'Still inside' is the synthesis's gloss. The Judgment itself says 'stilling the back… walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people.' The phrasing is clipped and a bit cryptic, and it sits near the short's own 'pause / stay with where you are now.' Nothing concrete to remember or send to a friend. Better: line 5, 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.' → 'Still your jaw,\nyour words make sense.' (15/19, so trim: 'Still your jaw,\nwords make sense.'). It is concrete, a little funny, true to the line, and answers the 'overthinking' hook. Or use the Hokusai Red Fuji painting the input offers, if painting fits the variety count here.

lessons.text:
Goose in a tree?
Find flat footing.
lessons.why: A goose can't grip a branch; in the wrong place it looks for a flat perch, and there is no fault.
lessons.feedback: True to line 4: the goose advances to the trees and perhaps finds a flat branch, no fault. It is concrete, a little funny, a good fit for the lit line, and it adds a new angle (being in the wrong place) to 'step by step'. One fix: 'flat footing' is alliteration the text doesn't have. The text's own 'a flat branch' is more concrete and fits in 18 characters: 'Goose in a tree?\nFind a flat branch.'

lessons.text:
The princess wore
the plainer dress.
lessons.why: The emperor's daughter dressed plainer than her attendant, and it resolves well.
lessons.feedback: True to line 5: the princess's sleeves were plainer than her attendant's, and it resolves well. Concrete and surprising, in the same vein as the approved 'guest, not inspector.' It adds to the short rather than repeating it. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
Lightning to see,
thunder to act.
lessons.why: Thunder over fire: abundance gives clear sight and the force to act at the same time, and that window does not last.
lessons.feedback: True to the Image ('Thunder and lightning both arrive') and its synthesis (clarity to see, force to act). The parallel is neat and plain. Two problems. The picture labels the lower trigram FIRE 火, not lightning, so the viewer has to make that jump in two seconds. 'Thunder to act' also leans on the short's own question 'What will you decide now?' instead of adding something new. It is also abstract rather than surprising. Stronger: line 2/4, 'So abundant are the screens that the Big Dipper is visible at midday' → 'So dark at noon\nyou see stars.' It is concrete and odd, and it adds the warning side of abundance after 'be the sun at noon.' Line 4 ends with meeting the hidden master in the dark, which makes it the kinder choice. If you keep the lines kind, match the label: 'Fire to see,\nthunder to act.'

lessons.text:
The wanderer burns
his own inn.
lessons.why: A guest who wrecks the shelter he was given loses his helper too.
lessons.feedback: True to line 3. Concrete, a little funny, and it gives the consequence of 'You're a guest. Act like one.' without repeating it. One small point: 'own' is not quite right, because the inn is not his, and the synthesis makes that the point. 'The wanderer burns\ndown the inn.' is more exact.

lessons.text:
Say it too often,
it grates.
lessons.why: Line 3, repeated penetration brings friction: repeating has a limit, past which the listener pushes back.
lessons.feedback: Line 3 says 'Repeated penetration. Friction.' Reading it as speech is fair given the Image's 'reiterates commands', though the app's synthesis reads the line as overthinking. It works well against the short. The copy says 'say it again' and asks 'What's worth repeating today?', and this answers with the limit. It is plain, a little funny, and something you would send to a friend. Keep it. One small option: 'Say it too often,\nit starts to grate.' reads more like speech, but it is 19 characters on line 2, so the current version is fine.

lessons.text:
Painters toast,
then talk shop.
lessons.why: Krøyer's artists at their party: the Image joins friends for discussion and practice, not only celebration.
lessons.feedback: True to the Image: 'joins with friends for discussion and practice.' 'Talk shop' is a plain, funny way to say discussion and practice. 'Painters' matches the Krøyer artists' party on screen, and it adds to 'share it' by saying joy with friends includes working together. One small gap: the canvas shows the toast, not the shop talk, so the second half comes from the text, not the picture. That is acceptable at a glance. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
Drop your faction,
more will gather.
lessons.why: Dissolving your own group supremely resolves well: dispersion creates accumulation, more than any faction could hold.
lessons.feedback: True to line 4: 'Dispersing one's group. Supremely resolves well. Dispersion creates accumulation.' It is counterintuitive and adds to a short whose copy is about reminding people of a shared origin. It lands at a glance. 'Faction' is slightly formal; 'Drop your own side,\nmore will gather.' is plainer if you want it. Otherwise glad to post.

lessons.text:
A lake holds only
so much water.
lessons.why: Water over the lake: knowing your capacity is what keeps you from flooding.
lessons.feedback: True to the Image, and it fits the trigrams picture (water above the lake) directly. Plain and concrete. It stays close to 'Where's your limit?' but gives the reason in a picture, so it still adds something. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
Truth even reaches
pigs and fish.
lessons.why: The Judgment opens with piglets and fish: real sincerity reaches even them.
lessons.feedback: True to the Judgment and its synthesis. Concrete, funny, and it answers the hook 'Can't get through to someone?' well. 'Truth' instead of 'sincerity' is close enough. Glad to post.

lessons.text:
Missed the king?
See the minister.
lessons.why: Not reaching the ruler, meeting the minister: in a small time the tier below is the right channel, no fault.
lessons.feedback: True to line 2 ('Not reaching the ruler, meeting the minister. No fault'). It is concrete, plain, a little funny, and it fits the short's 'small' theme without repeating the hook, meaning or question. Glad to post. Keep an eye on variety with 60, 61 and 63.

lessons.text:
Fine silk turns
to rags.
lessons.why: After completion, decay is slow and quiet, so the line says to stay watchful all day.
lessons.feedback: True to line 4. A concrete picture of slow decay that adds to 'stay alert' without repeating it. Glad to post. If there were room it could hint at 'watch all day,' but it works as it is.

lessons.text:
Almost across,
the fox gets wet.
lessons.why: The little fox has almost crossed and wets its tail: the last step is where it goes wrong.
lessons.feedback: True to the Judgment: the fox is the best-known image in the book and a fitting last word for the series. 'Almost across' echoes the hook ('So close to done?') a little, but the fox makes it a new thing. One small fix for precision: the book says the tail gets wet, and that detail is the joke. Try "Almost across,\nfox wets its tail." (14/18).

history.text:
Heaven on heaven:
it never stops.
history.why: Both trigrams are heaven, and the Image says heaven moves without ceasing.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('Heaven moves with inexhaustible vigor... strengthens without ceasing') and it fits the two HEAVEN trigrams. It is plain but a little abstract, and it mostly restates the short's 'begin / just mean it'. It would be stronger if the second line said what the viewer does, e.g. 'Heaven on heaven:\nit never stops.' kept, or 'Heaven never stops.\nNor do you.' Fine to post if nothing better comes.

history.text:
Frost underfoot:
ice is coming.
history.why: Line 1: small signs now tell you what is coming later.
history.feedback: Line 1 says 'Treading on frost. Solid ice is coming.' Concrete, a little ominous, and a real surprise next to a short about following well. It adds to the short. Glad to post.

history.text:
Without a guide,
let the deer go.
history.why: Line 3: chasing deer into the forest without a forester goes wrong, so let it go.
history.feedback: Line 3: chasing deer with no forester, 'better to let it go.' 'Guide' for forester is a fair plain word. It is concrete and fits 'boring beats bold' without repeating it. Good.

history.text:
A spring starts
under a mountain.
history.why: Water under mountain is a spring just coming out, the Image's picture of inexperience.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('A spring emerges beneath the mountain: inexperience'), but it only names the picture and never says what it means, so it risks the 'watchtower' problem: a viewer learns there is a spring, not what that has to do with youthful folly or asking once. Add the meaning, e.g. 'A new spring:\nit has to learn.' or pull in the Image's 'thoroughness', e.g. 'A new spring\ngoes slowly.' Or use line 6 instead (striking at inexperience fails, defending works).

history.text:
Uninvited guests?
Receive them well.
history.why: Line 6: three uninvited guests arrive; treat them with respect and it ends well.
history.feedback: Line 6: three uninvited guests, receive them with respect, it ends well. Concrete, a little funny, and a good twist on 'wait well'. Consider 'Three strangers show up?' to keep the book's specific number, but it works as is.

history.text:
Won the belt,
lost it by noon.
history.why: Line 6: a win taken by fighting is stripped away before the morning is out.
history.feedback: Line 6: 'awarded the champion's belt. By morning's end, stripped of it three times.' 'By noon' is a fair plain version. Concrete and funny. It illustrates 'pushing to the end costs you' without repeating the wording. Could add the 'three times' if it fits, but it is good.

history.text:
Unseen water
under the earth.
history.why: Accepted: water within the earth is the army, the people held in reserve.
history.feedback: Approved standard. It matches the Image and the EARTH over WATER picture.

history.text:
Friends at lunch,
holding together.
history.why: Accepted: Renoir's crowded table shows holding together at a glance.
history.feedback: Approved standard. The painting makes the point at a glance.

history.text:
Thick clouds,
but no rain yet.
history.why: The Judgment's picture: dense clouds gather, and the rain has not come yet.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('Dense clouds but no rain'), but it restates the short's hook ('Everything's ready, nothing happens?') and meaning ('not yet') as a picture, so the lesson adds nothing new. Use a line instead. Line 3 is concrete and funny: 'Wheel off the cart,\nthe couple glaring.' (18/18). Line 5 also works: 'Get rich along\nwith your neighbours.'

history.text:
The tiger's tail:
it does not bite.
history.why: Accepted: tread carefully and even the tiger does not bite.
history.feedback: Approved standard: concrete, surprising, true to the Judgment.

history.text:
No flat plain
without a slope.
history.why: Line 3: good times include downhill stretches; don't worry about it.
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('No level plain without slopes'), but on its own it reads like a proverb, and the useful part of the line, 'Do not worry about these certainties', is missing. Try 'Every plain slopes.\nDon't worry.' or 'No going\nwithout return.' Line 4 ('Not wealthy, yet sharing with neighbours') is another option that fits the short's 'peace is contact'.

history.text:
The great departs,
the small arrives.
history.why: The Judgment: in a standstill the great goes and the small comes, the reverse of Peace.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment, and back to back it mirrors Peace nicely, but on its own it is cryptic: a new viewer cannot tell what 'the great' and 'the small' are. Use line 5 instead, which is specific and human: ''What if it fails?'\nTie it down.' (the mulberry-shoot line). Avoid line 6 ('first standstill, then joy'), because it would echo 13's 'First weeping, then laughter.'

history.text:
First weeping,
then laughter.
history.why: Line 5: fellowship can start in tears and end in laughing together.
history.feedback: Line 5: 'first with weeping and wailing, then laughter.' Human, a little surprising, and it adds to 'keep it open' without repeating it. Good.

history.text:
A big cart and
somewhere to go.
history.why: Line 2: having a lot is fine when it is put to use and has a direction.
history.feedback: True to line 2 ('A great cart for loading. Having somewhere to go.'), and it is concrete. The line break after 'and' is awkward, and the point (wealth needs a direction) is left to the viewer. Try 'Big cart, loaded,\nsomewhere to go.' It is close to 'use it to put things right' but adds the picture, so it is acceptable.

history.text:
A mountain inside
the earth.
history.why: Mountain under earth: something big that keeps itself low, the Image of modesty.
history.feedback: True to the Image and the EARTH over MOUNTAIN picture, but like the rejected 'watchtower' it only names the shape and leaves the meaning to the viewer. The second half of the Image is more concrete and not in the short's copy: 'reduces what's excessive and increases what's lacking'. Try 'Level the heaps,\nfill the holes.' or say the meaning outright: 'A mountain\nkept below ground.'

history.text:
Shout about it
and it goes wrong.
history.why: Line 1: proclaiming your enthusiasm is adverse.
history.feedback: Line 1: 'Proclaiming one's enthusiasm. Adverse.' 'Shout about it' is a plain, slightly funny version. It adds a warning to 'give it a shape' without repeating it. Good.

history.text:
Heaven on heaven:
keep going.
history.why: Heaven moves without ceasing, and the realized person strengthens without ceasing: the two HEAVEN trigrams say keep going.
history.feedback: True to the Image (heaven moves without ceasing; strengthens without ceasing). But it is abstract, and 'keep going' sits close to the short's 'says: begin' / 'Just mean it', so it adds little. 'Heaven on heaven' also reads a bit cryptic. Better: a line lesson that pushes against 'begin', e.g. line 1 'Hidden dragon:\ndon't act yet.' (true to 'The hidden dragon. Do not act.'), which is concrete and a small surprise after a short that says go. If it stays a lines lesson, make it plainer: 'Heaven never stops.\nNeither do you.' (the first line is exactly 18 characters).

history.text:
A new spring
goes step by step.
history.why: A spring emerging under the mountain is inexperience; the Image's answer is to proceed with thoroughness.
history.feedback: Mostly true: the Image has a spring under the mountain and 'proceeds with thoroughness'. But 'step by step' is a loose gloss of 'thoroughness', and 'a new spring' reads first as the season, not water. It does not land in two seconds. Better: line 2, 'Let the kid\nrun the house.' (from 'The young one manages the household. Resolves well.'). It is concrete, a little funny and true, it adds to the short's ask-once copy, and it fits the lit-line picture.

history.text:
The cart breaks,
the couple glare.
history.why: Line 3: the cart throws its spokes and husband and wife glare at each other; pushing when held back breaks things.
history.feedback: True to line 3 (the cart throws its spokes; husband and wife glare) and concrete, with a little humour. The weakness: it is two images with no point, so the viewer does not get the 'pushing when held back breaks things' the writer intends. A stronger ending for a short whose hook is 'Everything's ready, nothing happens?' is line 6, where the rain finally comes and advancing turns bad: 'The rain comes:\nnow stop pushing.' (both lines under 18). That pays off the hook. To keep line 3, the phrasing is fine as it is.

history.text:
Each plain slopes.
Don't worry.
history.why: Line 3: no level plain without slopes; do not worry about these certainties.
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('No level plain without slopes... Do not worry about these certainties'), and a good turn after the short's upbeat 'keep it moving': good times tilt, and that is fine. 'Each plain slopes.' sounds stiff; people don't talk that way. Plainer: 'No flat ground\nwithout a slope.' It keeps the book's image in words people use; the 'don't worry' can go, or try 'Every road dips.\nDon't worry.'

history.text:
Stuck times suit
the careless.
history.why: The Judgment: standstill favours inferior people and does not support the noble one, so feeling blocked is not your failing.
history.feedback: It comes from the synthesis ('blocks the people who care... the ones who don't care are doing fine'), but 'careless' means sloppy, not 'people who don't care', so it misstates the point. 'Stuck times suit' is stiff. The Judgment's own words are plainer: 'The great leave,\nthe small arrive.' Better still is line 5 (standstill ends, and the great person says 'What if it fails? What if it fails?'): 'Standstill ends.\nWhat if it fails?' It is concrete, human and a little funny, and it does not repeat 'hold back' or 'turn down'.

history.text:
Big cart, loaded,
somewhere to go.
history.why: Line 2: a great cart for loading, with somewhere to go: wealth needs a direction.
history.feedback: True to line 2 (a great cart for loading, somewhere to go, no fault), concrete, and it fits the lit-line picture. It doesn't repeat the copy ('people see', 'put things right'). But it is flat: the viewer sees a loaded cart and no point, because 'wealth needs a direction' stays unsaid. A plainer version with the point: 'A full cart needs\nsomewhere to go.' (16 and 16 characters). Or line 1, where trouble looks like opportunity, would add an edge to 'doing better than everyone'.

history.text:
Level the heaps,
fill the holes.
history.why: The Image: the mountain within the earth reduces what is excessive and increases what is lacking.
history.feedback: True to the Image (reduces what's excessive, increases what's lacking, weighing to distribute evenly). 'Heaps' and 'holes' are a fair concrete rendering and suit the picture of the mountain sunk inside the earth. It is plain and short, and it adds a new idea (redistribution) to a short about credit and finishing quietly. It ends well. I would post it. A minor risk: the link to 'modesty' is left to the picture. Fine as is.

history.text:
Heaven never
takes a day off.
history.why: The Image: heaven moves with inexhaustible vigor, and the realized person strengthens without ceasing. (Not a line lesson: 1-2-3 would be three line lessons in a row. The critic's 'Heaven never stops.' is 19 characters.)
history.feedback: Checked against the Image: 'Heaven moves with inexhaustible vigor. The realized person accordingly strengthens without ceasing.' The idiom is plain and a little funny, it fits HEAVEN over HEAVEN, and it adds persistence to a short whose copy only says 'begin'. Line lengths are 12 and 16 characters. It is not a 9 because it leaves out the second half of the Image: heaven doesn't stop, so the person doesn't either. The picture carries that only if the viewer makes the link. Keep it.

history.text:
Teachers don't
chase students.
history.why: The Judgment: it is not I who seek the youth, the youth seeks me. (Not the suggested line 2: 3, 4 and 5 would be three line lessons in a row.)
history.feedback: The Judgment says: 'It is not I who seek the inexperienced youth, the inexperienced youth seeks me.' The synthesis has almost the same words ('The teacher doesn't chase the student'). It is plain, concrete and easy to share. The short's copy uses the other half of the Judgment ('ask once / asking twice is shopping'), so this adds the half that comes before it without repeating it. The one weakness is that the Judgment page is the same source the meaning lines already came from, so it is less of a surprise than a line lesson. Line 5, where the clueless youth is the one who does well, would be more surprising, but the kind-variety rule blocks a line lesson here. Keep it.

history.text:
The rain comes:
now stop pushing.
history.why: Line 6: the rain the hexagram waited for arrives, and advancing now is adverse; it answers the hook 'Everything's ready, nothing happens?'

history.text:
No flat ground
without a slope.
history.why: Line 3: no level plain without slopes. Good times tilt, and that is normal.
history.feedback:
Almost word for word from line 3 ('No level plain without slopes'). It answers the hook 'Good times, now what?' well, since good times tilt, and it doesn't repeat 'keep it moving' or 'contact, not a vacation'. It is concrete, the kind of thing a person would say, and the book's own image, so it is not an invented metaphor. The viewer needs a moment to get from ground to good times, which keeps it at 8 rather than 9. If you want it quicker, the line's second clause, 'No going
without return.', is an option, but the slope version is the more vivid of the two.

history.text:
The great leave,
the small arrive.
history.why: The Judgment: standstill is peace in reverse, and the great departs while the small arrives. (Not line 5: 11-12-13 or 12-13-14 would be three line lessons in a row.)
history.feedback:
Verbatim from the Judgment, but it is too cryptic, the same problem as the rejected 'watchtower'. A viewer who has never heard of the hexagram doesn't know who 'the great' and 'the small' are, or where they are leaving from and going to. In two seconds it reads as a riddle. It also only mirrors Peace's Judgment, and this series is watched back to back. The Image ('heaven and earth do not interact') would repeat the hook's 'no one's talking', so don't swap to a lines lesson built on that. Better: keep the Judgment but say who loses, e.g. 'Bad times: the
small-minded win.' or 'Good people lose
ground for now.' Or, if the variety rule can be satisfied by changing 13's kind, use line 5, which is concrete and human: the standstill ends and the great person still says 'what if it fails?' Something like 'It ends. Still ask:
what if it fails?' (18/17 chars).

history.text:
A full cart needs
somewhere to go.
history.why: Line 2: a great cart for loading, with somewhere to go; wealth needs a direction.
history.feedback:
True to line 2 ('A great cart for loading. Having somewhere to go.'). It is concrete, fits a lit line, and adds direction to a short whose copy is about visibility and fixing things. Two issues. (1) 'needs' turns the line's plain statement, that you have the cart and you have the destination, into advice the text doesn't give, so it leans toward a maxim. (2) As a result it reads a little like a slogan rather than something surprising. A plainer phrasing that stays with the text: 'A big cart, full,
and a road to go.' or 'Load the cart.
Know where to go.' Either is fine. The current one is close to postable. Fix the 'needs' and it is an 8.

history.text:
Wheels come off,
the couple glares.
history.why: Line 3: the cart throws its spokes and husband and wife glare at each other; when something structural breaks, people on the same side turn on each other.
history.feedback: Line 3 says exactly this: the cart throws off its spokes, husband and wife glare at each other. The rules check passes: 6 words, 16 and 18 characters. It is concrete and a little funny, in the same register as the approved 'guest, not an inspector'. It adds something new after the short's 'not yet / work on yourself' copy and fits the lit-line picture. One small option: 'Spokes fly off,' is closer to the text, but 'Wheels come off' reads faster. I would post it.

history.text:
The ones who care
get blocked.
history.why: The Judgment: inferior people do not support the noble one's sustained orientation; the standstill blocks the people who care while the ones who don't do fine. (Not a line lesson: 11-12-13 would be three line lessons in a row.)
history.feedback: It is true to the app's Judgment commentary ('it specifically blocks the people who care'), but the Judgment text on screen reads 'Of inferior people... The great departs, the small arrives', so the sentence and the picture do not quite match. It is also abstract and a bit bleak. It comes right after 'What will you turn down?' and deflates the ending instead of adding a concrete fact. Better, still a judgment lesson to keep 11-12-13 varied: take the Judgment's own image, 'The great leaves,\nthe small arrives.' (16/17 chars, 6 words). A reader can check it against the page, and it shows why things stall. If a line lesson becomes possible after reordering, line 5 is the best material: the great person says 'What if it fails? What if it fails?' as the standstill ends. Avoid the Image (heaven and earth not talking), because the hook already says 'no one's talking'.

history.text:
A full cart,
a place to go.
history.why: Line 2: a great cart for loading and somewhere to go; you have the capacity and the destination.
history.feedback: It is true to line 2 (a great cart for loading, somewhere to go), plain, and fits the lit-line picture. The rules check passes (6 words, 12 and 14 characters). The problem is that it lands soft: 'a full cart, a place to go' comes across as a generic good omen, so a new viewer learns little, and it does not connect to the short's 'people see / put things right / what would you fix first?'. Two ways to lift it: make the point sharper and more active, e.g. 'Load the big cart.\nKnow where it goes.' (17/18 chars); or use line 1, which is more surprising at the start of abundance and ties to 'fix first': the book says stay clear of harm, e.g. 'Rich now? Keep\nclear of harm.' The Klimt painting is available, but its own note says it does not carry 'putting things right', so keep it as a line lesson.

history.text:
The great leaves,
the small arrives.
history.why: The Judgment's own words, 'The great departs, the small arrives': the viewer can check it against the page on screen, and it says why things stall. (Judgment, not line 5, so 11-12-13 are not three line lessons in a row.)
history.feedback:
True to the Judgment ('The great departs, the small arrives') and it passes the checker (17 and 18 chars, 6 words). It fits the Judgment page, and it doesn't repeat the hook ('no one's talking'), meaning ('hold back', 'bad deal') or question ('turn down'). The problem is that it is cryptic in the same way as the rejected watchtower lesson. A viewer who doesn't know the hexagram can't tell whether 'the great' and 'the small' are people, things or amounts, so in two seconds they learn a riddle, not a fact. 'Leaves' against 'arrives' also reads like translation, not talk. Better: say who they are, using the synthesis ('it specifically blocks the people who care'): 'Good people leave,
small ones arrive.' (17/17). Or, closer to the Judgment's first clause: 'Small people in,
good people out.' (16/16). If the kind can change without making 11-12-13 three line lessons, line 5 is the surprising material: the standstill ends and the great person says 'What if it fails?' twice, e.g. 'It ends. Still:
what if it fails?' (15/18). Avoid a 'lines' lesson on Heaven over Earth ('stop talking'), because it would repeat the hook.

history.text:
Rich now? Keep
clear of harm.
history.why: Line 1: 'No interaction with harm. Not a fault.' When abundance starts, the first job is to stay away from what can hurt you. That answers 'what would you fix first?' without repeating it.
history.feedback:
Line 1 does say 'No interaction with harm. Not a fault.', and 'Rich now?' is fair context for Great Possession, so the lesson is true to the text. It passes the checker (14/14 chars, 6 words) and fits the lit LINE 1 picture. It has three problems. (1) 'Keep clear of harm' is generic advice any viewer already knows. The line only surprises through the synthesis: at the start of abundance, trouble looks like opportunity, and the hard part is saying no. (2) 'Rich now?' is a third question in a short that already opens with one ('Doing better than everyone around you?') and ends its main part with one ('What would you fix first?'). It echoes the hook and doesn't close the short. (3) It doesn't really follow 'fix first'. The meaning is about putting things right, and 'keep clear' is a step sideways from that. Better options: carry the synthesis point on line 1, e.g. 'Harm will look
like a good deal.' (13/17, 'a good deal' is the plain version of 'looks like opportunity'), or 'Say no to the
wrong friends.' Or use line 2, which is the most concrete image in the hexagram and would be good to rewatch: 'A big cart, and
somewhere to go.' (15/16, 7 words). Line 5 (trust both ways at the peak) is another candidate: 'At the top: trust
that goes both ways.' Check the kinds on 13 and 15 before you settle on a line lesson here. The Klimt painting reads as wealth, not putting things right, so it adds nothing beyond the hook.

history.text:
Follow the child,
lose the grown-up.
history.why: What you follow costs you something: holding the small one means letting the grown one go.
history.feedback: True to line 2 ('Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.'). It is concrete and a little surprising, and it doesn't repeat the copy about stopping at nightfall. Two problems: 'Follow' is not the line's verb ('attached to'), and a cold viewer could take it as parenting advice. The line's point is the trade, and that doesn't come through. Try 'Hold the child,\nlose the grown-up.' (15/18), which is closer to the text and states the trade. Line 3 is the mirror of line 2 and supports the opposite choice. Line 2 is still the better pick, because it gives no verdict and just shows the cost.

history.text:
Plan three days,
check three days.
history.why: The Judgment's 'three days before, three days after' gives the repair a concrete measure: think before and after.
history.feedback: The Judgment says 'three days before the new start, three days after'. 'Plan' and 'check' are the synthesis's reading ('deliberate on both sides'), not the text's words. It is concrete and fits the Judgment page. But it overlaps with the copy's 'Rushed repairs don't hold', and 'plan three days, check three days' sounds like a productivity tip. Closer to the page: 'Three days before,\nthree days after.' (17/16). Or try line 1, which is more surprising: 'Fix your father's\nmess: no blame.' (17/14), from 'If there is a son to examine it, no fault falls'.

history.text:
Teach and protect,
without limit.
history.why: Earth over the lake is the person who reaches down to teach and protect without running out.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('teaches with inexhaustible thought and protects the people without limit'). But it reads like a mission statement. It is abstract, it doesn't touch the picture (EARTH over LAKE), and nobody would send it to a friend. The Judgment's eighth-month deadline is already in the copy ('every spring has an autumn'). Better, as a lit line 3: 'Too comfortable?\nWorry a little.' (16/15), from 'Comfortable approach. No direction is supported. Once one worries about it: no fault.' It is concrete and a little funny, and it adds to 'go, but plan'. Or line 1/2, 'joint approach': 'Don't approach\nit alone.'

history.text:
Look like a guest,
not an inspector.
history.why: Approved: at line 4 the supported move is to be the sovereign's guest, observing with a visitor's courtesy.
history.feedback: Approved standard. True to line 4's synthesis (guest, not inspector). It is concrete and a little funny. It extends the copy's 'go and look' without repeating it.

history.text:
Make the penalties
clear to all.
history.why: Fire over thunder is lightning then thunder: the kings made penalties clear, because a penalty everyone sees is structure.
history.feedback:
True to the Image ('made penalties clear and established the law'). But 'penalties' is legal, sounds like a government notice and has nothing to do with the copy's personal blockage. The sentence also never says lightning or thunder, so it doesn't use the FIRE over THUNDER picture. The line texts are far better here. Line 4: 'Arrowheads in
the dried meat.' (13/15), from 'Biting through dried meat on the bone. Finding metal arrows... resolves well'. It is a vivid picture of the hard case inside the problem and fits 'bite down'. Or line 5: 'Gold inside the
tough meat.' If you keep the lines kind, name the images: 'First the lightning,
then the thunder.' is 19/15, too long for line 1.

history.text:
The purest grace
is plain white.
history.why: The ornament hexagram ends with no ornament: plain white grace, no fault.
history.feedback:
True to line 6 ('Plain white grace. No fault.'). It ends the polish theme well, and the lit top line fits. 'The purest grace' is a little mannered (the synthesis's word, not the text's). Plainer: 'It ends in
plain white.' or 'Best grace:
plain white.' Line 4 is more surprising and more fun: 'Not an attacker:
a suitor.' (16/9), from 'A white horse, as if winged. This is not an assailant — it is a suitor.'

history.text:
The bed breaks at
the legs first.
history.why: Collapse starts at the base, the part nobody looks at.
history.feedback: True to line 1 ('Splitting the bed at the legs'). 'First' is earned, because lines 2 and 4 go on to the frame and the skin. It is concrete and visual, fits the lit bottom line and backs the copy's 'help those below you' without repeating it. Glad to post.

history.text:
Seven days, and
it comes back.
history.why: The Judgment names the cycle: on the seventh day, return comes.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('On the seventh day, return comes'). But 'it comes back' largely repeats the copy's 'Return says: energy returns', and 'it' is vague. Seven days is the only new thing. Line 1 adds more: 'Best return: you\ndidn't go far.' (16/14), from 'Returning from not far away... Supremely favorable'. It is concrete, a little surprising, and fits 'rushing back'. Line 4 is another option: 'Mid-crowd, you\nturn back alone.'

history.text:
Innocent, yet
the ox is taken.
history.why: Innocence does not protect you from misfortune; it only means the misfortune is not your fault.
history.feedback: True to line 3 (tethered ox taken, innocence meets misfortune). It is concrete and pushes back usefully against the copy's 'stop faking, and it works'. But 'Innocent, yet' is a bit literary, and without 'not your fault' it may not land in two seconds. Plainer: 'Did no wrong,\nstill lost the ox.' (12/16). Line 5 is also strong and surprising: 'Not your illness:\ndon't treat it.' (16/14).

history.text:
Study the past,
build character.
history.why: Heaven held inside the mountain: the person stores up strength by studying the words and deeds of the past.
history.feedback: True to the Image, but it sounds like a school poster: abstract, no picture, no surprise. It also pulls against the copy's 'go public / don't eat at home', so it doesn't close the short well. Use a line instead. Line 4: 'Cap the calf's\nhorns early.' (14/11), from 'The young bull's headboard. Supremely resolves well.' It is prevention in one concrete image. Or line 5: 'The boar keeps its\ntusks, not its bite.'

history.text:
Stop staring at
someone's plate.
history.why: Line 1 sets down its own spirit tortoise to gape at someone else's meal: envy traded for self-sufficiency.
history.feedback: True to line 1 (setting aside your own spirit tortoise to watch another's jaws: adverse). It is concrete and funny, and it adds envy to the copy's 'watch your mouth'. It drops the book's twist that you already had your own food source. If there is room: 'You have your own.\nStop staring.' Fine as is.

history.text:
Stand alone,
without fear.
history.why: With Hokusai's wave towering over the boats, the Image's water above the trees asks you to stand alone without fear.
history.feedback: True to the Image, but abstract, and the link to Hokusai's wave is weak: the boats aren't alone, and the copy says 'move now', not 'stand alone'. Line 6 matches the wave: 'In over your head,\nbut not your fault.' (18/18), from 'Wading too deep, the water covers the head. Adverse. No fault.' It is a surprise, plainly said, and lands at a glance over the painting. It could also be a lit line 6 if the painting slot is better used elsewhere. Line 2 is an alternative: 'Old tree, new shoot\nat the root.'

history.text:
In double danger,
stay sincere.
history.why: In the abyss inside the abyss, only sincerity in the heart works, not strength or speed.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment, but 'sincere' is vague and the sentence is abstract. A viewer learns nothing they can picture. The copy's 'next small step' already covers the practical side. Line 4 is the concrete one: 'Wine and rice,\nthrough the window.' (13/18), a care package in the abyss, no fault. Line 3 is also stronger and fits 'one problem after another': 'Pit ahead, pit\nbehind: don't move.' (14/18).

history.text:
At sunset, don't
party or wail.
history.why: Drumming and singing and lamenting old age are both adverse responses to the setting sun.
history.feedback: True to line 3 (drumming and singing vs lamenting old age, adverse). The 'both wrong' reading is the synthesis's, which is fair. It is concrete, a little funny, fits the burnout copy and the lit line. One small change: cite lines[2].synthesis too, since 'don't do either' comes from there.

history.text:
Influence that
leads to marriage.
history.why: The Judgment skips attraction and goes to commitment: taking a wife resolves well.
history.feedback:
Loosely true to the Judgment ('Taking a wife resolves well'). But it is a clunky noun phrase, not a sentence, and it sounds like a label. It also has little to do with the copy's 'make room'. Line 1 would land better: 'It starts in
the big toes.' (12/15), 'Influence in the big toes', concrete and a little funny. So would line 4: 'Waver, and your
friends waver.' (15/13), from 'companions follow your thinking', which ties to 'already decided'. If you keep the Judgment: 'Good time to
take a wife.' is plainer, but it drifts toward prediction.

history.text:
No game in this
field. Move.
history.why: Persistence in the wrong place is wasted: a field with no game.
history.feedback: True to line 4 ('A field with no game'). 'Move' is the synthesis's word. It is concrete and funny, and a useful counterweight to 'keep doing'. The break 'this / field.' is a little awkward. 'No game here.\nMove fields.' (13/12) reads cleaner. Glad to post either way. Series note: 8 of these 16 are line (50%, over the 40% target), and 3 are lines.

history.text:
Hold the child,
lose the grown-up.
history.why: Line 2 shows the cost of following: attached to the small child, you lose the mature one.
history.feedback: Line 2 says 'Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.' The lesson is true to it, and it's concrete and adds to a short about resting after dark. The problem is that a new viewer reads it as advice about babies. Nothing on screen says the child and the grown-up are what you choose to follow. 'grown-up' also softens the joke. The synthesis wording is plainer and a little funnier: 'Grab the kid,\nlose the adult.' A version that states the point: 'What you follow\ncosts you something.' Either would get it to 8.

history.text:
Three days before,
three days after.
history.why: The Judgment puts time on both sides of the new start: three days before it, three days after.
history.feedback:
The Judgment does say 'three days before the new start, three days after', but the lesson drops 'the new start', so the viewer is left with two time phrases and no point. It has the same problem as the rejected 'watchtower' line: a fact without a takeaway. The point of 'take your time on both sides' is also already in the meaning line 'Rushed repairs / don't hold.' Better options: keep the judgment and state the point ('Three days to plan,
three to check.' is 18/15 characters, close to the synthesis's 'deliberate on both sides'). Or switch to line 1 ('Fixing what your
father let rot.' is 16/15 and concrete), or line 6 ('Serve no king.
Honour your work.').

history.text:
Too comfortable?
Worry a little.
history.why: Line 3: a comfortable approach supports nothing, but once you worry about it there is no fault.
history.feedback: Line 3: 'Comfortable approach. No direction is supported. Once one worries about it: no fault.' The lesson is faithful, plain and a little funny, and it answers the question 'What will you prepare now?' well. It doesn't repeat the copy's spring/autumn idea. Good to post.

history.text:
Lightning shows,
thunder hits.
history.why: Fire over thunder: first see the problem clearly, then bite down with force.
history.feedback:
The Image says 'Lightning and thunder', and the synthesis says 'first the clarity, then the force.' So it's true, but as written it only describes weather. The point (see it clearly, then act) is left for the viewer to work out, and 'thunder hits' repeats the copy's 'bite down.' The picture's label says FIRE, not lightning, which is a small mismatch. Say the point in plain words: 'See it clearly,
then bite down.' (15/14). Or use the Image's own instruction: 'Make the rules
clear to all.' Another option is line 4, which is concrete and surprising: 'Bite the bone,
find arrowheads.'

history.text:
Not an attacker:
a suitor.
history.why: Line 4: the white horse rushing in is not an assailant but a suitor, so what looks like a threat is an offer.
history.feedback:
Line 4 says the white horse 'is not an assailant — it is a suitor', and the lesson is true to that. The trouble is that it drops the horse. With only a lit line on screen, the viewer doesn't know what the attacker or the suitor is, so the lesson reads as a riddle. It also doesn't connect to this short's topic (polish vs. decisions). The synthesis wording is plainer: 'Not an attack,
a proposal.' (14/11). Or keep the image: 'A white horse?
It's a suitor.' Also consider the Image line, which fits the short's topic better: 'Grace for small
things, not fights.' (it clarifies everyday affairs but does not decide disputes).

history.text:
At the solstice,
close the passes.
history.why: Thunder under the earth: at the turning point the ancient kings closed the passes and nobody travelled, so the return could come.
history.feedback: The Image says the kings 'closed the passes at the solstice. Merchants did not travel.' The lesson is true and concrete, and that ancient kings shut the roads is a small surprise. But it mostly repeats the copy's 'Rest. Only rushing stops it', 'passes' is a word some viewers will stumble on, and it doesn't say what thunder under earth means for the trigram picture. Plainer: 'At the turn,\nall roads close.' or 'At the solstice,\nnobody travels.' (16/15). Variety: 24 and 25 are both 'lines', so 23 must not be 'lines' too.

history.text:
Feed each thing
in its season.
history.why: Thunder under heaven: the ancient kings nourished all beings in step with the seasons, not forcing growth.
history.feedback: The Image says the kings 'nourished all beings in alignment with the seasons.' The lesson is true and plain, but it reads like a generic proverb. It doesn't connect to 'without pretense', the short's topic, and it doesn't use the thunder-under-heaven picture. It's forgettable. Line 5 is more surprising and fits innocence: 'An illness without pretense. Do not medicate. There will be happiness.' Try 'Honest illness?\nNo medicine.' (15/12). That also breaks up the lines/lines run with 24.

history.text:
Cap the calf's
horns early.
history.why: Line 4: a board on the young bull's horns, supremely good, is restraint put in place before there is harm.
history.feedback: Line 4: 'The young bull's headboard. Supremely resolves well.' The lesson is concrete and a little surprising, and it teaches prevention as a new idea after the copy's 'go public'. 'calf' is a fair plain word for young bull. Good to post.

history.text:
In over your head.
Not your fault.
history.why: Line 6, over Hokusai's wave: wading too deep, the water covers the head. Adverse, but no fault.
history.feedback: Line 6: 'Wading too deep, the water covers the head. Adverse. No fault.' The synthesis supports reading 'no fault' as 'not your fault' ('It went badly' and 'you were wrong' are separate). With Hokusai's wave it lands at a glance, it's a little funny, and it answers the hook 'Under too much weight?' well. One small thing: the painting entry has no year, and the card needs one (c. 1831).

history.text:
Wine and rice
through a window.
history.why: Line 4: in the abyss, a jug of wine and a basket of rice handed through the window is enough, and in the end no fault.
history.feedback: Line 4 has wine, rice and clay vessels handed through the window, and 'in the end, no fault.' The lesson is true, concrete and memorable, and it answers the question 'What's the next small step?' But on its own it's close to the rejected 'watchtower' kind of lesson: a picture with no point stated, so a first-time viewer doesn't know why rice through a window matters. Add 'enough' or 'small': 'Enough: rice\nthrough a window.' (12/17), or 'Small help,\nthrough a window.'

history.text:
Real influence
ends in marriage.
history.why: The Judgment says taking a wife resolves well: influence is meant to land in commitment, not stay as attraction.
history.feedback:
The Judgment only says 'Taking a wife resolves well.' 'Real influence ends in marriage' is the synthesis's gloss turned into a general rule. It overreaches, it sounds preachy, like a dating proverb, and 'Real' is a mannered word here. It doesn't fit the short's topic (making room, listening) either. The line texts are much better: influence moves up the body, from the big toes (line 1) to the jaws, cheeks and tongue (line 6). 'It starts
in the big toes.' (9/15) is concrete, funny and true. Or line 6: 'Last, it reaches
the tongue.' If you keep the Judgment, say only what it says: 'Taking a wife:
it goes well.'

history.text:
Follow the kid,
lose the adult.
history.why: Line 2: attached to the small child, losing the mature one. Whatever you follow costs you something else.
history.feedback: True to line 2 ('Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.'), concrete, and a little funny. It is 15/15 characters and passes the checker. Two problems. 'Follow the kid' reads as an instruction, but the line only describes a trade and gives no verdict. 'The adult' also sounds like literal childcare. The trade idea is also cut off from this short, which is about stopping work at nightfall. Try making it read as a trade, e.g. 'Hold the child,\nlose the grown-up.' (15/17), or 'Grab the kid,\nlose the adult.' Either is an 8 if it keeps the no-verdict tone.

history.text:
Plan three days,
check three more.
history.why: The Judgment gives three days before the new start and three days after: deliberate on both sides of a repair.
history.feedback: Close to the Judgment ('three days before the new start, three days after'), but 'plan' and 'check' are the commentary's reading, not the book's words. The main problem is that it repeats the short's second meaning line, 'Rushed repairs / don't hold', which already comes from this Judgment. It adds nothing, and 'three days' means nothing to someone new to the book. Use a line of the hexagram instead. The lines about the father's and mother's decay are the surprising material. Line 1: 'Fix Dad's mess,\nclear his name.' (14/14): the son's repair means no fault falls on the father. Line 2: 'Mom's mess?\nGo gently.': the mother's decay needs a lighter hand than the father's.

history.text:
See it clearly,
then act.
history.why: Fire over thunder, lightning then thunder: first the clarity, then the force.
history.feedback: True to the Image commentary ('first the clarity, then the force'), but it is abstract, and it never names what the picture shows. FIRE over THUNDER is lightning and thunder. The approved 7 works because it names the two images ('Unseen water / under the earth'). Plainer and tied to the picture: 'Lightning first,\nthen thunder.' (15/12). Better still, use line 4. Biting dried meat and finding metal arrowheads is the most vivid text in the hexagram and fits the short's 'bite down' copy: 'Metal in the meat:\nkeep biting.' (18/12). The Hodler Woodcutter painting is also available if a painting is needed nearby.

history.text:
A white horse?
It's a suitor.
history.why: Line 4: the white horse that looks like an attacker is a suitor. Something striking arriving is not always a threat.
history.feedback: Glad to post. It is concrete, surprising, a little funny, and quoted almost word for word from line 4 ('This is not an assailant - it is a suitor'). It also adds something to a short about polish versus decisions. One small gap: nothing says the horse looks like a threat, so the twist lands a little softer than it could. Optional version: 'Not a raider.\nA suitor.' Or keep the horse: 'A white horse:\nnot an attack.' The current text is fine.

history.text:
At the solstice,
nobody travels.
history.why: Thunder inside the earth: at the turning point the ancient kings closed the passes, and merchants and the ruler stayed home.
history.feedback:
True to the Image ('closed the passes at the solstice. Merchants did not travel. The ruler did not tour'), and a real, concrete historical fact. But it does not fit its picture. The trigrams show EARTH over THUNDER, and the sentence never says thunder is underground. It also mostly restates the short's second meaning line ('Rest. Only rushing / stops it.'), which comes from the same Image. Either name the images ('Thunder under earth:
stay put.' is 19 characters, so trim it to 'Thunder underground:' plus a second line, still too long, so maybe 'Thunder below:
kings stayed home.' 14/18), or switch to a line. Line 1 is the best verdict in the hexagram and adds a new idea: 'Didn't go far?
Easy to come back.' (14/18). Line 4: 'Turn back alone
in the crowd.'
