history.text:
If not upright,
don't go ahead.
history.why: The Judgment: if not upright, there is calamity, and going forward is not supported.
history.feedback: Accurate to the Judgment, but it repeats the short: 'be straight / stop faking and it works' already makes this point. 'Upright' is stiff and 'don't go ahead' sounds like a warning notice. Nothing is new, nothing is concrete, and it is not something anyone would send to a friend. The lines of this hexagram are much stronger. Line 5, an illness you didn't cause: do not medicate, happiness will come ('Not your illness?\nDon't medicate.', 17/15), which is surprising. Line 3, the tethered ox taken by a passer-by ('Did nothing wrong,\nstill lost the ox.', 18/18), which says innocence does not protect you.

history.text:
Small help through
a window counts.
history.why: Line 4: wine and rice in clay vessels handed through the window, and in the end no fault. In the abyss the smallest help is enough.
history.feedback: True to line 4 (wine, rice and clay vessels handed through the window, no fault). It ends well after 'What's the next / small step?'. But the break splits the phrase in the middle ('Small help through / a window counts'), and 'small help' and 'counts' are vaguer than the text. The concrete objects are the charm. Try 'Wine and rice\nthrough a window.' (13/16), or 'Rice through a\nwindow: no fault.' (14/17). Either keeps the picture and reads in one glance.

history.text:
Taking a wife:
it goes well.
history.why: The Judgment says only this: taking a wife resolves well. Influence that works ends in a bond.
history.feedback: Quoted from the Judgment, but it lands badly. After a short about making room and not deciding in advance, 'Taking a wife: it goes well' is a non sequitur. It sounds like a fortune about marriage, it assumes a male viewer, and it teaches nothing in two seconds. Switch to a line. The hexagram moves up the body from the toes to the tongue, which is concrete and a little funny. Line 1: 'It starts\nin the big toes.' (9/16). Line 4: companions follow your thinking ('Waver, and friends\nwaver with you.', 18/15), which ties back to the short's question about deciding. Line 4 as a line kind also breaks the judgment/judgment rhythm with 25.

history.text:
Grabbed the kid,
lost the adult.
history.why: Line 2: attached to the small child, losing the mature one. No verdict, only the trade: following one thing means letting go of another.
history.feedback: True: line 2 reads 'Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.' and the synthesis says almost exactly 'You grabbed the kid and lost the adult.' Mechanics pass (16/15 chars, 6 words). It is concrete, a little surprising, and it adds to a short about stopping for the day: following one thing costs you another. What holds it under 8 is 'Grabbed the kid'. Read cold under a lit line, it sounds like a snatching or a custody fight, and the viewer has to work out that it describes a choice. Plainer and closer to the line text: 'Keep the child,\nlose the adult.' (15/15) or 'Hold the little one,' is too long, so use the first. Keep the kind (line).

history.text:
Wind at the base:
stir the people.
history.why: Wind beneath the mountain is rot from below; the Image answers it by stirring the people and feeding character, not by patching the surface.
history.feedback:
True to the Image ('stirs the people and nourishes character'), and the mechanics pass. It does not land, though. 'Wind at the base' only makes sense if you already know it means rot from below, and 'stir the people' is abstract and sounds political. Next to 'rushed repairs don't hold', a viewer learns nothing they can picture. The line texts are the concrete material here, a child fixing a parent's mess. Line 1: 'Fix dad's mess,
clear his name.' (14/14): the son's repair means no fault falls on the father, which is surprising and true. Line 2 also works: 'Mom's mess:
don't push hard.' (11/16). Check the variety rule against 17 (line) and 19 before switching to a line. If 19 is also a line, go with judgment instead: 'Three days before,
three days after.' (18/17).

history.text:
Lightning first,
then thunder.
history.why: FIRE over THUNDER is lightning and thunder: you see it, then you feel it. The ancient kings made penalties clear before they used force.
history.feedback:
The Image only says 'Lightning and thunder'. The order 'first, then' comes from the app's synthesis ('you see it and then you feel it'), so it is supported, but loosely. The problem is that the sentence gives a weather fact and leaves out the point, which only the 'why' carries: make penalties clear before using force. The trigram label also reads FIRE, not lightning, so the picture and the text don't quite line up. Better, still as lines: 'Make the rules
clear first.' (14/12), true to 'made penalties clear'. The strongest material is in the lines, though. Line 4: 'Bit the dried meat,
hit an arrowhead.' (18/16) is concrete, surprising, and fits 'bite down'. Line 5: 'Gold inside
the dried meat.' (11/15) also works.

history.text:
Thunder below:
kings stayed home.
history.why: Thunder within the earth: at the solstice the ancient kings closed the passes, merchants did not travel and the ruler did not tour.
history.feedback:
True: 'closed the passes at the solstice... the ruler did not tour the regions.' Mechanics pass. It is concrete and a little surprising: at the turning point, even kings stay put. It overlaps with the short's own meaning, though ('Rest. Only rushing stops it' comes from this same Image), so it restates more than it adds. 'Thunder below' also says less than the picture already shows. Adding the solstice detail makes it more specific and more interesting: 'Solstice:
kings stayed home.' (9/17). Or change the takeaway with line 1: 'Didn't go far:
best possible sign.' (14/18) or 'Turn back early:
the best return.' (16/16), which adds something new ('catch it early') after 'What are you rushing back to?'.

history.text:
Thunder under sky:
feed in season.
history.why: Thunder beneath heaven: the ancient kings nourished all beings in line with the seasons, not forcing growth but matching it.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('nourished all beings in alignment with the seasons'), and the mechanics pass. 'Feed in season' is abstract, though. A viewer can't picture it and can't connect it to a short about faking and performing, and 'Thunder under sky' just repeats the picture. The line texts hold this hexagram's surprising material. Line 3: 'Did nothing wrong,\nlost the ox.' (18/13): the tethered ox is taken, and innocence doesn't protect you from misfortune. That is concrete and a little unfair, which is why people remember it. Line 2 is another option: 'Don't plow\nfor the harvest.' (10/16). Check neighbours 24 and 26 before switching to a line.

history.text:
Wine and rice
through a window.
history.why: Line 4: wine, rice and clay vessels handed through the window; in the end, no fault. In the abyss, a small plain offering is enough.
history.feedback:
True: line 4 is 'A jug of wine, a basket of rice... handed through the window. In the end, no fault.' Mechanics pass. It is concrete, odd enough to remember, and it follows 'What's the next small step?' well. On its own, though, the sentence gives only the image, not what it means. Without 'no fault' or 'that's enough', the viewer may read it as a riddle, which is close to the rejected watchtower case. Keep the image and add the verdict or the size, within 18 characters: 'Wine and rice
through a window' leaves the point to the picture. Try 'A small meal via
a window: enough.' (16/17) or 'Just food through
a window. No fault.' (17/19, too long, trim to 'a window: no fault' =18). Close to 8 once the point is on screen.

history.text:
Lake on the peak:
low over high.
history.why: LAKE over MOUNTAIN puts the low thing above the high thing, water above stone; that is the picture of influence. (Not a line: 30 and 32 are accepted line lessons, so a line here would make three in a row.)
history.feedback: True to the synthesis ('the low thing above the high thing'), and the mechanics pass. 'Low over high' is the same kind of cryptic shape-reading as the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower'. The viewer sees LAKE over MOUNTAIN and gets told the geometry again, and the point behind it (make room, receive through emptiness) is already the short's meaning. A line lesson is ruled out because 30 and 32 are lines. Use the judgment: 'Taking a wife resolves well.' Try 'This one ends\nin a wedding.' (13/12) or 'Influence that\nends in marriage.' (14/17). It is plain and a little surprising, and it adds something new: the book cares whether influence becomes a commitment.

history.text:
Keep the child,
lose the adult.
history.why: Line 2: attached to the small child, losing the mature one. Whatever you follow costs you something else.
history.feedback: True to line 2 ('Attached to the small child. Losing the mature one.'). Mechanically fine (15/15 chars, 6 words). The problem is it doesn't land in two seconds: without the idea of following, a viewer takes 'child' and 'adult' literally and doesn't know what is being traded. It also leaves the short's theme (go in at nightfall, rest) and adds nothing to it. 'Keep' is weaker than the book's 'attached to'. If you keep this line, write 'Hold the child,\nlose the grown-up.' (15/17), which is a bit more concrete. A better choice for this short is line 4, 'Following gains a catch' plus the warning not to hold on to it, e.g. 'You caught it.\nDon't cling to it.' That fits a short about knowing when the day is done.

history.text:
Three days before,
three days after.
history.why: The Judgment gives the repair three days on each side of the new start: time to think before and to check after.
history.feedback: It quotes the Judgment directly and fits the Judgment page. But 'three days before, three days after' what? The new start is cut, so a newcomer only gets a riddle, much like the rejected watchtower lesson. It also restates the meaning line 'Rushed repairs don't hold' more than it adds to it. A plainer version: 'Plan three days,\ncheck three days.' (16/17; the synthesis supports it). Better still is line 1 as a line lesson, the most surprising material here: fixing the father's decay means no fault falls on the father, e.g. 'Fix dad's mess,\nclear his name.' (15/15). It's concrete, a little unexpected and easy to send to someone.

history.text:
Make the rules
clear first.
history.why: Lightning and thunder: the ancient kings made penalties clear and established the law. Clarity comes before force.
history.feedback:
The Image says 'made penalties clear and established the law', so the rule part is true. 'First' comes from the synthesis ('first the clarity, then the force'), which is allowed. But it reads like an office memo: it's abstract, and the lightning and thunder that the trigram picture shows (FIRE over THUNDER) never appear, so the words and the picture don't meet. If you keep the Image, tie it to the picture: 'Lightning, then
thunder: see, then hit' is too long, so try 'Clear laws first,
then the penalty.' (17/16). The hexagram's best material is the lines, though. Line 4, 'Biting through dried meat on the bone. Finding metal arrows', fits a short about a stubborn blocker: 'Arrowheads
in the dried meat.' The 'bite down' copy also makes the Hodler Woodcutter painting a real option.

history.text:
Solstice:
kings stayed home.
history.why: Thunder within the earth: at the solstice the ancient kings closed the passes and the ruler did not tour the regions.
history.feedback: True: the Image says the kings closed the passes at the solstice and the ruler did not tour. It's concrete and a little surprising, and it backs up the short's 'Rest. Only rushing stops it' with a historical fact, not a repeat. Two small problems. The 'Solstice:' opener has the same clipped label-then-colon shape as the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower', and the trigram picture (EARTH over THUNDER) isn't in the words. Plainer: 'At the solstice,\nkings stayed home.' (16/18), or 'Passes shut,\nkings stayed home.' Either would make it an 8.

history.text:
Not straight?
Don't go anywhere.
history.why: The Judgment: if not upright, there is calamity, and going forward is not supported.
history.feedback: The Judgment supports it ('If not upright, there is calamity. Going forward is not supported'). But it repeats the short almost word for word: the hook is about hiding your reasons and the meaning is 'be straight'. 'Don't go anywhere' also reads as the everyday 'stay tuned', and the whole thing sounds like a scolding. The lines are the surprising material here. Line 3 (the tethered ox taken by a traveler; innocence doesn't protect you): 'Did nothing wrong,\nstill lost the ox.' (17/18). Line 5 (an illness not of your making; do not medicate; there will be happiness): 'Not your fault?\nDon't medicate.' Both add something the short doesn't say. Line 3 is the stronger ending.

history.text:
Food through
a window: no fault
history.why: Line 4: wine and rice handed through the window, and in the end no fault. In the abyss, a small plain offering is enough.
history.feedback:
True to line 4 (wine, rice, clay vessels handed through the window; in the end no fault). It's concrete and odd enough to stick, and it answers the short's question 'What's the next small step?' well. But 'no fault' is book jargon a newcomer won't read as anything, and the missing full stop is inconsistent. Drop the verdict and keep the image: 'Rice and wine,
through a window.' (14/17). Or say what it means: 'In the pit, send
food through a window' is too long, so try 'Stuck? Pass food
through a window.' (16/17).

history.text:
This one ends
in a wedding.
history.why: The Judgment: taking a wife resolves well. The book cares whether influence becomes a commitment.
history.feedback:
It rests on 'Taking a wife resolves well', and it's plain and a little funny. But 'This one ends in a wedding' overstates the text: the book says marrying goes well, not that the story ends in marriage. It also reads like a prediction, close to fortune-telling, and 'this one' has nothing to refer to on the Judgment page. It also has no link to the short's 'make room / already decided'. The famous and surprising part of Influence is the body sequence in the lines. Line 1: 'It starts
in the big toes.' Line 6 (influence in the jaws, cheeks and tongue) against a short about being already decided: 'Last stop:
jaws and tongue.' Or 'Toes first,
tongue last.' (10/11), which a viewer gets at a glance with the lit line. If you keep the Judgment, write 'Taking a wife:
it goes well.' (14/13).

history.text:
Last to leave?
Don't move yet.
history.why: The tail of a retreat is the worst place to move; line 1 says do not act.
history.feedback:
True to line 1 ('Retreat at the tail... Do not act'). But it opens with a question right after the short's own question, and it stays on the leaving theme the short already covers (hook 'Time to walk away?', question 'What are you ready to leave?'). 'Last to leave' is also looser than 'at the tail'. It works as advice but is not a picture a viewer would send to a friend. Better: line 3 is concrete and surprising, 'Leaving? Take your
people with you.' (keep the servants and concubines). Or line 2, 'Tied with oxhide.
No one can loosen it.' If you keep line 1, drop the question: 'At the back of
a retreat: stay put.'

history.text:
Ram hits hedge.
Horns get stuck.
history.why: Line 3's ram shows that force alone gets power stuck.
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('The ram butts the hedge and entangles its horns'). Concrete and a little funny. After the question 'What won't you do with it?' it shows what force alone gets you. The headline clip ('Ram hits hedge') is fine at this length. Ready to post.

history.text:
Three audiences
in a single day.
history.why: The Judgment's picture of progress: a lord received three times in one day.
history.feedback:
True to the Judgment. But a modern viewer reads 'audiences' as crowds, not meetings with a lord, so it does not land in two seconds. It is also an event, not a takeaway, and it echoes the hook 'Finally getting recognized?' without adding much. Better: line 4 is funny and specific, 'Don't advance
like a squirrel.' ('Progressing like a squirrel... strained'). Or line 2, 'Help can come
from grandmother.' If you keep the Judgment, say 'Seen by the king
three times a day.'

history.text:
The light sinks
into the earth.
history.why: Fire under earth is the image of the name: brightness gone underground.
history.feedback: Close to word for word from the Image ('Brightness enters the earth'; synthesis: 'The light sinks into the earth'), and it fits the trigram picture. But the short's meaning already says 'Keep your light inside', so this restates the name and adds nothing new. Better: line 5, Prince Ji, who hid his sanity at the tyrant's court. It is the most surprising, concrete thing in the hexagram: 'A prince played mad\nto stay alive.' (line kind, LINE 5).

history.text:
Too strict beats
too much giggling.
history.why: Line 3: sharp scolding still ends well, giggling ends in friction.
history.feedback: True to line 3 (sharp scolding resolves well, giggling ends in friction), and funny and concrete. The problem is that it contradicts the short, whose hook is 'Too many rules at home?' and whose meaning is 'skip the rules'. Coming right after that, 'Too strict beats' reads as a reversal, not an addition. Either keep it and rework the copy, or pick a line that fits: line 5, 'The king comes home\nas family.' ('As a king approaches his family. Do not worry'). A Chardin painting is also available for this hexagram if the painting share needs it.

history.text:
Not an attacker,
a suitor.
history.why: Line 6: what looked like a threat was someone coming to propose.
history.feedback: True to line 6 ('Not an assailant — a suitor'). Surprising and a little funny, and it adds to 'start small / stay different'. It fits the lit line. It could carry more of the line's picture, e.g. 'A cart of ghosts?\nNo, a suitor.' (16/12 chars), but as written it is ready to post.

history.text:
Water stuck on
a mountaintop.
history.why: Water over mountain is the picture of obstruction: water that cannot flow.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('Water upon the mountain'; synthesis: 'it can't flow, it just sits there'). Plain, and the same pattern as the approved 'Unseen water under the earth'. Small snag: a viewer knows water runs down mountains, so 'stuck on a mountaintop' may read as odd rather than as the picture. The hexagram's most memorable material is the repeated line pattern 'Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: praise.' Line 1 as a line lesson, 'Blocked ahead?\nTurn back. Get praised.', adds something the short doesn't say (its meaning is 'ask for help').

history.text:
Riding with a load
invites thieves.
history.why: Line 3: carrying the old burden into freedom makes you a target.
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('Carrying a burden while riding in a carriage. Inviting thieves'). Concrete and a little funny, and it goes well with the short's 'let the grudges go', since the old load is the grudge. It is exactly 18 chars on line 1, which is fine. Optional plainer version: 'A load on your back\nin a carriage' is too long, so keep it as is.

history.text:
Walk alone,
find a companion.
history.why: Line 3: three walking lose one, one walking finds a companion.
history.feedback: Half of line 3. Dropping 'three walking lose one' removes the surprise, and 'Walk alone, find a companion' on its own reads like a greeting card. Keep both halves: 'Three lose one.\nOne finds a friend.' (14/17 chars). That is the actual line and makes the decrease/increase point at a glance.

history.text:
Now you can cross
the great river.
history.why: The Judgment says crossing the great river is supported: a time for big moves.
history.feedback:
True to the Judgment, but it repeats the short: the hook is 'Door's open, still hesitating?' and the meaning is 'Increase says: go now'. 'Cross the great river' is also stock I-Ching phrasing that means nothing to a new viewer. Replace it. Best: line 3, 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault', as 'Even bad luck
can add to you.' Or line 5, 'Be kind.
Don't ask for more.' ('Do not ask — supremely resolves well'). Or line 6's warning, 'An unsteady heart
loses it all.'

history.text:
Tell your own
town first.
history.why: Before a breakthrough, the Judgment says notify your own city.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('Notify your own city'). Practical and a little surprising, and it adds to the short's 'say it openly' by saying who to tell first. Plain. Ready to post.

history.text:
Looks wonderful.
Don't let it in.
history.why: La Tour's cheat's table shows the attractive thing the Judgment says not to take in.
history.feedback: Taken from the judgment synthesis ('looks wonderful... Don't let it in'), so it is commentary, not the text. It also repeats the short three times over: the hook 'Something shiny', the meaning 'Charm can be the warning', and the question 'too good to be true'. The painting already carries that idea, so the sentence adds nothing. Either let the painting carry it with a line that adds something, e.g. line 1, 'Brake it early.\nA lean pig kicks.', or use the Judgment's own words, 'She is strong.\nDon't marry her.' (the risk there is that it reads as sexist without context). Also note 44 and 45 are both paintings, two in a row, while the series aims for 10%. Consider switching one of them.

history.text:
One handshake,
laughter again.
history.why: Line 1: at a gathering, one handclasp restores laughter; Bruegel's wedding shows the crowd.
history.feedback: True to line 1 ('one handclasp restores laughter'). Warm, plain, and a good answer to the hook 'bracing for arguments'. But it is paired with the wrong picture: Bruegel's Peasant Wedding shows a crowd, not a handshake, so the viewer looks for the handshake and doesn't find it. Make it a line lesson (LINE 1) with the same sentence, which also removes the back-to-back paintings (44, 45). Or keep the painting and use the Judgment/Image: 'A crowd needs\na center.'

history.text:
Wood grows
inside the earth.
history.why: Wind (wood) under earth: a tree pushing up through soil, slowly.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('Within the earth, wood grows'). Same shape as the approved 'Unseen water under the earth', and it fits the trigrams. But the short's meaning ('Small steps, piled up') already gives the point, so this mostly labels the picture. 'Inside the earth' also reads slightly odd; 'A tree pushing up\nthrough the soil' (17/15) is plainer. For more surprise, line 3: 'Pushing up into\nan empty town.'

history.text:
Stuck, even in
a golden carriage.
history.why: Line 4: oppression can come with comfort, and the line says it ends.
history.feedback: True to line 4 ('Oppressed in a gilded carriage... There is an end'). Concrete and a little surprising after a hook about not being heard. But the writer's own 'why' names the point, that it ends, and the sentence leaves it out. Add it: 'Stuck in a gold\ncarriage. It ends.' (15/17 chars).

history.text:
Towns change.
The well stays.
history.why: The Judgment: the town may change but the well does not.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment and plain. But the short's meaning already says 'The water is always there', so this largely repeats it. The hexagram's most striking line is line 3, the only place the book sounds sad: 'The well is cleaned but no one drinks. This is my heart's sorrow.' As a line lesson: 'Clean well.\nNo one drinks.' (11/13). It adds something new and ends the short on a feeling.

history.text:
Leaving? Take your
people with you.
history.why: Line 3: a tangled retreat goes well if you keep your dependents with you instead of cutting them loose.
history.feedback:
Line 3 says 'keeping servants and concubines resolves well' and the synthesis says 'bring them along', so the lesson is true to the text. It is concrete and a little surprising. 'Leaving?' repeats the hook ('Time to walk away?'). If you want it sharper: 'Tangled exit? Keep
your people close.' Fine to post as is.

history.text:
Seen by the king
three times daily.
history.why: The Judgment's picture of real recognition: the lord is received three times in a single day.
history.feedback:
'Three times daily' misreads the text. The Judgment says three audiences 'in a single day', one exceptional day, not every day. The Judgment also never names a king. The lesson only describes the recognition that the hook ('Finally getting recognized?') already covers, so the viewer gets no takeaway. Better, line 5: 'Stop counting
wins and losses.' Or line 4, which is concrete and funny: 'Don't advance
like a squirrel.' If you keep the Judgment: 'Horses, and three
audiences in a day.' (check the length).

history.text:
A prince acted mad
to stay alive.
history.why: Line 5: Prince Ji hid his sanity at the tyrant's court, the book's own example of hiding your light to survive.
history.feedback:
The line 5 synthesis names Prince Ji, who faked madness at the tyrant's court. A real story gives the meaning ('Keep your light inside') a face, and that is surprising. 'Acted mad' can be read as 'got angry'. 'A prince faked
madness to live.' is less ambiguous.

history.text:
Whoever feeds them
holds the family.
history.why: Line 2: the one who stays in and feeds everyone is the center of the family, which Chardin's mother at the table shows at a glance.
history.feedback:
Line 2 ('attending to the nourishment within', synthesis: 'the person who feeds everyone') plus the Judgment synthesis on holding the center supports it. Chardin's mother serving at the table shows it at a glance, and the lesson moves the short away from rules. 'Holds the family' is a touch abstract. 'Whoever feeds them
is the center.' would be more literal, but this is postable.

history.text:
Water stuck? Then
work on yourself.
history.why: The Image: water on the mountain can't flow, so the realized person turns inward to build character.
history.feedback:
True to the Image. But 'Water stuck?' is awkward, and 'work on yourself' is the abstract self-help line. The short's meaning ('The wall is the lesson') already says it, so the lesson repeats it. The picture shows WATER over MOUNTAIN, but the lesson never mentions the mountain. Better, lines 1/3/4 (forward: obstruction, coming back: praise, return, connection): 'Blocked? Coming
back earns praise.' If you keep the lines kind: 'Water on a mountain
can't flow.' (trim it to 18 characters).

history.text:
Two small baskets
are enough.
history.why: The Judgment: when you have less, a humble offering given sincerely is enough.
history.feedback:
True and concrete ('Two small baskets may be used for the offering'). But 'are enough' restates the meaning 'give what you can', and a cold viewer doesn't know the baskets are an offering. Try 'Two small baskets
make an offering.' Or go to line 3, which is more surprising: 'Three lose one.
One finds a friend.'

history.text:
Even bad luck
can add to you.
history.why: Line 3: 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' Misfortune can become growth.
history.feedback:
True to line 3 ('Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.'). But it is abstract and sounds like a greeting card. 'Add to you' is not how people talk, and 'bad luck' borders on the fortune language the rules avoid. Plainer: 'Bad things can
make you grow.' Stronger, line 5: 'Be kind. Don't
ask what you get.' This is the highest verdict for kindness that doesn't ask, and it follows 'move toward good' well.

history.text:
Brake it early.
A lean pig kicks.
history.why: Line 1: check the small, harmless-looking thing at once, because a tethered lean pig still kicks and struggles.
history.feedback:
True, and the lean pig is funny and memorable. But 'Brake it' has no antecedent. A viewer reading for two seconds doesn't know what 'it' is, and 'brake' is odd as a verb. Try 'Check it early:
lean pigs kick.' or 'Tie it up early.
A lean pig kicks.' Check the variety rule too: 42, 44 and 45 are all line lessons. If 43 is also a line lesson, 43 to 45 break it.

history.text:
One handshake,
laughter again.
history.why: Line 1: after confusion, one handclasp restores laughter, so don't worry about the arguments.
history.feedback:
True to line 1 ('one handclasp restores laughter. Do not worry'). It answers the hook ('bracing for arguments') warmly and concretely, and ends the short well. Postable. Optional: 'One handshake,
and the laughter's back.' is longer than 18 characters, so keep it as is.

history.text:
A tree pushing up
through the soil.
history.why: The Image: wood growing within the earth, rising by yielding and adding small things.
history.feedback:
True to the Image ('Within the earth, wood grows'), in the same register as the approved 'Unseen water under the earth'. But the picture labels the lower trigram WIND 風, not wood, so a viewer sees 'wind' and reads 'tree'. It also describes the image without adding much to 'Small steps, piled up'. More surprising, line 3: 'Pushing up into
an empty town.'

history.text:
Stuck in a gold
carriage. It ends.
history.why: Line 4: oppressed even in a gilded carriage, but 'there is an end'.
history.feedback:
True to line 4 ('Oppressed in a gilded carriage... There is an end'). The image is concrete and 'It ends' is a good close. The line break 'gold / carriage' splits the noun phrase and reads awkwardly. Try 'Trapped in gold?
It ends.' or 'A gold carriage
can trap you too.' (that drops 'It ends'). Note that 47 and 48 are both line lessons, so 49 must be another kind.

history.text:
The well is clean.
No one drinks.
history.why: Line 3, the only sad line in the book: the well is cleaned and no one drinks, 'my heart's sorrow'.
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('The well is cleaned but no one drinks. This is my heart's sorrow'). It is plain, concrete and sad. It turns the hook ('Good things just out of reach?') around, which is surprising. You could post it as is. It sits at the top of the batch with 36.

history.text:
Three audiences
in one day.
history.why: The Judgment's picture of progress: on one exceptional day the lord is received three times, and the rewards come faster than he can take them in.
history.feedback: The Judgment does say 'granted audience three times' in a single day. The problem is the word 'audiences': today it means a crowd watching a show, so a new viewer will read it as a performer's busy day and not as being received by the king. It also leaves out the horses, which are the most vivid part of the Judgment. And it pulls against the short, which says 'character first' and asks 'What are you like up close?'. A picture of rewards pouring in doesn't finish that thought. Plainer judgment wording: 'Seen by the king\nthree times a day.' (16/18). Better, as a line lesson: line 4, 'Progressing like a squirrel. Strained.' is concrete and a little funny, and it ties to the short's 'up close' question: 'Don't get ahead\nlike a squirrel.' (15/16).

history.text:
On a mountain,
water can't flow.
history.why: The two trigrams, WATER over MOUNTAIN, show why this is obstruction: water on a mountaintop has nowhere to go.
history.feedback: It is in the Image synthesis ('it can't flow, it just sits there'). But viewers know water on a mountain runs downhill, so the claim reads as wrong and makes them stop and think. That is the opposite of landing in two seconds. The Image text itself only says 'water upon the mountain'. It also adds little to 'The wall is the lesson'. Use line 1 instead: 'Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: praise.' It is surprising, specific and true, and it answers 'Hit a wall?' with something new: 'Turning back\nearns praise.' (11/12). Or line 4, 'Coming back: connection': 'Blocked? Go back\nfor friends.' The line kind also helps variety.

history.text:
Two small baskets
make an offering.
history.why: The Judgment: in a time of less, a humble offering of two small baskets is accepted.
history.feedback: The Judgment says it: 'Two small baskets may be used for the offering.' It suits the Judgment page. It is close to the short's meaning 'give what you can', but it gives the concrete picture behind it, so it adds something. 'make an offering' ends flat. The point is that the small offering is enough, so say that: 'Two small baskets\nare enough.' (16/10). That would be an 8. Another option, more surprising, if the variety quota allows: line 3, 'Three people walking lose one. One person walking finds a companion': 'Three lose one.\nOne finds a friend.' (14/17).

history.text:
Be kind. Don't
ask what you get.
history.why: Line 5: kindness that doesn't ask about the return gets the highest verdict, 'supremely resolves well'.
history.feedback:
The source supports it: line 5 has 'kind heart... Do not ask — supremely resolves well', and the synthesis reads that as not asking about the return. But it is an abstract moral command, and the line break 'Be kind. Don't / ask what you get.' cuts the second sentence in half, which reads awkwardly on screen. It sounds like a poster and gives the viewer nothing concrete. Keep the line and fix the phrasing, for example 'Be kind.
Don't keep score.' (8/17). Better: line 3, 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' is the surprising line of this hexagram: 'Bad luck
can still add up.' or 'Even bad events
can increase you.' (16/16).

history.text:
A lean pig kicks.
Tie it early.
history.why: Line 1: the small thing that looks harmless still struggles, so restrain it at the first sign.
history.feedback: Line 1 has the tethered lean pig that kicks and struggles and the metal brake, and the synthesis says to check it at the first sign. The lesson is concrete, a little funny, and teaches the hexagram's point, stop the small thing early, in one picture. It adds to 'Charm can be the warning' and doesn't repeat it. Small point: the text says the pig is already tethered and the verb is 'brake', but 'Tie it early' matches the meaning. Post as is.

history.text:
Go see the person
who matters.
history.why: The Judgment: while things are rising, use the time to go and see the great person, without worrying.
history.feedback:
It comes from the Judgment synthesis ('Go see the person who matters'), but it is vague: which person, and why? A new viewer learns nothing concrete about Pushing Upward, and it reads like generic career advice. It also doesn't answer the short's question 'What can you add today?' Better, as a line lesson: line 3, 'Pushing upward into an empty town', is strange and specific, and the synthesis reads it as no one is in your way: 'Climbing into
an empty town.' (13/13) or 'No one is
in your way.' If it has to stay a judgment lesson, use the Judgment's own words, which are plainer and a little surprising: 'Don't worry.
Go south.' (12/9).

history.text:
A lake with
no water.
history.why: The two trigrams, LAKE over WATER, show the water drained out below the lake: the empty lake is the book's picture of oppression.
history.feedback: The Image says it word for word: 'The lake without water: oppression.' It fits the trigram picture well, LAKE with WATER below it, the water drained out underneath. A new viewer gets a clear picture of what oppression looks like in the book. It gives the source picture behind the short's 'hold your purpose' without repeating it, much like the approved 'Unseen water under the earth.' A little flat. If you want more bite, the Judgment line 'Having words — they are not believed' is concrete, but it is too close to the hook ('Speaking up and nobody listens?'), so keep this one.

history.text:
The sun comes up
over the earth.
history.why: FIRE over EARTH is the book's picture of progress: light rising over the ground, the image behind 'brighten your own character' (line was blocked: 33 and 34 are line).
history.feedback:
Accurate: the Image says 'Brightness emerges above the earth' and the synthesis says 'the sun coming up over the earth'. It fits the FIRE over EARTH picture, and 'The sun comes up' is 16 characters, so it passes the checker. The problem is that it only puts the picture into words. Unlike 'Unseen water under the earth' it has no turn, and it doesn't connect to the short's point (character first). A viewer learns what the trigrams are, not what Progress says. Better: switch to judgment, which the variety rule allows (33 and 34 are line). The Judgment is concrete and surprising: 'Three audiences
in one day.' or 'Horses pour in,
three audiences.' This adds the reward side of progress to the character-first meaning. If it stays lines, give the sun a point, for example 'The sun rises;
let yours show.' Check that against the Image's 'brightens their own character' so it doesn't read as mannered.

history.text:
Southwest, yes.
Northeast, no.
history.why: The Judgment gives two plain verdicts on direction before it says to see the great person: when blocked, some ways are open and some are not (line was blocked: 38 and 40 are line).
history.feedback: The Judgment does say 'The southwest is supported. The northeast is not supported.' But for someone who doesn't know the I-Ching it is cryptic. With no context the compass directions mean nothing, and it has the same weakness as the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower.' Nobody learns a real thing in two seconds. It also has nothing to do with the short's 'ask for help'. The Judgment's other point (see the great person) would repeat the meaning, so drop judgment here. Line is blocked (38 and 40 are line), so use lines: WATER over MOUNTAIN, where the Image and synthesis say the water can't flow and just sits there. For example 'Water stuck\non a mountain.' or 'Water on a\nmountain: stuck.' This picture shows the obstruction at a glance and sets up the short's 'the wall is the lesson.'

history.text:
Two small baskets
are enough.
history.why: The Judgment says two small baskets may be used for the offering: when you have less, a small offering is enough.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('Two small baskets may be used for the offering'). The synthesis supports reading it as 'enough': 'when you have less, bring less.' It is concrete, plain and fits the hook 'Having less than before?' Its weak point is that it largely restates the short's meaning line 'give what you can', so it adds an image but not a new idea. The Judgment page doesn't show baskets either, so the words carry the whole picture. Still worth keeping as the judgment lesson, and it keeps 40-41-42 varied. A small gain: 'Two small baskets\nwill do.' is more like speech. For a real surprise, line 3 ('Three lose one;\none finds a friend.') is the best material in Decrease. It is only usable if 40 or 42 moves off line kind.

history.text:
Even bad events
can increase you.
history.why: Line 3, the surprising line of Increase: 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.'
history.feedback: True to line 3 ('Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.'). It is the surprising line and fits the lit-line picture. It adds a lot beyond 'go now / see good, move toward it', and it ends the short with a twist. It loses points for 'increase you', which is awkward English that no one says out loud. Plainer: 'Even bad events\ncan make you grow.' (17 characters) or 'Bad luck can\nstill help you grow.' With that fix it would be an 8.

history.text:
A tree grows up
through the earth.
history.why: EARTH over WIND (wood) is the Image's 'within the earth, wood grows': the picture behind small things piled up until they are tall (line was blocked: 44 and 45 are line; 'Don't worry' repeats the short's meaning).
history.feedback:
True to the Image ('Within the earth, wood grows'). The synthesis also has 'a tree growing inside the earth, pushing up through soil'. It works well with the trigram picture: it explains why the label says WIND (wind is also wood), and slow growth underground answers the hook 'Growing slower than you want?' It stops short of an 8 because, like 35, it describes the picture rather than making a point, and 'through the earth' only just fits (18 characters). Tie it to the pace: 'A tree grows
under the ground.' is plainer. 'Wood grows slowly
inside the earth.' also works, but check it against the Image's wording. For more surprise, line 3 ('Pushing upward into an empty town' → 'You climb into
an empty town.') is the stranger, more memorable line. Line is blocked here (44 and 45 are line), so that is an option only if a neighbour changes.

history.text:
Three audiences
in one day.
history.why: The Judgment shows what progress looks like when it comes: horses given in abundance and three audiences with the king in a single day.
history.feedback: The Judgment does say this: 'In a single day, granted audience three times.' The problem is the word 'audiences'. A new viewer reads it as a crowd watching, not as meetings with a lord, so the line does not land in two seconds. It also shows only the reward, which the hook ('Finally getting recognized?') already implies. Fix 1, keep the judgment and name who is giving the audience: 'Seen by the lord\nthree times a day.' (16/18). Fix 2, better: use line 4, 'Progressing like a squirrel. Sustained orientation: strained.' It is concrete and a little funny, and it fits the short's 'character first' point: 'Don't get ahead\nlike a squirrel.' Check that the commentary's reading of the squirrel (a greedy, grabbing climber) supports this.

history.text:
Water stuck
on a mountain.
history.why: WATER over MOUNTAIN: water on top of a mountain can't flow and just sits there, the book's picture of obstruction.
history.feedback:
The Image says 'Water upon the mountain: obstruction', and the synthesis says 'it can't flow, it just sits there'. The line is plain and matches the WATER over MOUNTAIN picture. But it is closer to a caption than a lesson: it restates the hook 'Hit a wall?' as a picture and teaches nothing new. The line texts are more surprising. Lines 1, 3, 4 and 6 all read 'Going forward: obstruction. Coming back: ...', and line 1 ends in 'praise': 'Going on: stuck.
Coming back: praise.' (16/19; cut to fit, e.g. 'Go on: stuck.
Come back: praise.' 13/17). Line 2, 'It is not a personal matter', would also work: 'Blocked again?
It isn't personal.' (14/18). Either one adds to the 'ask for help' meaning without repeating it.

history.text:
Two small baskets
will do.
history.why: The Judgment says two small baskets may be used for the offering: when you have less, a small offering is enough.
history.feedback:
The Judgment says 'Two small baskets may be used for the offering.' It is concrete and a little surprising, and it fits the Judgment page. Two problems. First, without the word 'offering' the viewer doesn't know what the baskets are for, so 'will do' only half lands. Second, it partly repeats the meaning line 'give what you can'. Fix 1: 'Two small baskets
are offering enough.' (17/20, too long) or 'A small offering
is enough.' (16/10). Fix 2, better and more surprising: line 3, 'Three people walking lose one person. One person walking finds a companion.' → 'Three walk, lose one.
One walks, finds one.' (needs trimming to 18) or 'Three lose one;
one finds a friend.' (15/18). It is funny, specific, and new next to the short's copy.

history.text:
Even bad events
can make you grow.
history.why: Line 3: 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' Misfortune can be what increases you.
history.feedback:
Line 3 does say 'Increased through unfortunate events. No fault.' But 'can make you grow' is generic self-help language that could come from any poster. It loses what is specific to the line, and it doesn't connect to this short's hook and question about hesitating and moving toward the good. Options: (a) keep line 3 but say it concretely and plainly, e.g. 'Bad luck
can add to you.', which keeps the book's word 'increase' and drops the cliché. (b) Better, use line 6, which is the surprising warning: 'No one increases this one. Someone even strikes. The heart is not constant.' → 'Heart keeps changing?
No one adds to you.' (needs trimming to 18). That answers 'still hesitating?' directly. (c) Use the lines kind with the Image: 'See good, move toward it' is already in the copy, so the Image's other half, 'correct faults upon having them', would add something: 'See a fault,
fix it right away.'

history.text:
A tree grows
inside the earth.
history.why: EARTH over WIND (wind is also wood): the Image's wood growing within the earth, pushing up through soil before anyone sees it, which answers the hook about slow growth.
history.feedback: The Image says 'Within the earth, wood grows'. The line is plain, concrete, and answers the slow-growth hook without repeating 'Small steps, piled up'. The weak point is the picture: the lower trigram will be labelled WIND 風, so the viewer reads EARTH over WIND and then a sentence about a tree. That gap costs the two-second read. The fix is to label it WOOD 木, or WIND/WOOD, for this short. If the label can't change, use line 3, which is strange and memorable: 'Pushing upward into an empty town.' → 'Climbing into\nan empty town.' (13/14) as a line lesson. It is also the same shape as the approved #7 lesson ('Unseen water under the earth'). That is fine alone, but check that the neighbouring hexagrams don't also use lines.

history.text:
The petty change
only their faces.
history.why: Real change goes deep; the petty only swap faces, the line's contrast with the tiger and leopard.
history.feedback: True to line 6, and the tiger/leopard contrast is good material. The wording breaks it, though: 'The petty change' reads first as a noun phrase (small coins), and 'the petty' as a noun for people is old-fashioned. A viewer has to parse it twice. Name the people plainly and set them against the leopard, e.g. 'Some change deep.\nSome, just faces.' Or use line 5, 'Change like a tiger:\nno proof needed.' Also check that 48 is not a line lesson, because 49 and 50 are both line.

history.text:
Too heavy a load:
the legs break.
history.why: A caldron asked to carry more than it was built for breaks and spills the duke's meal.
history.feedback: True. 'Too heavy a load' comes from the synthesis; the line itself only says the legs break and the duke's meal spills on him. Plain, and it fits the hook. It leaves out the funniest, most concrete part: the duke covered in his own dinner. Better: 'The legs snap:\ndinner on the duke' (14/18) or 'The legs break.\nThe duke wears it.'

history.text:
First fear,
then laughter.
history.why: The Judgment puts terror and laughter in sequence: the shock comes, then the laugh.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment (terror, terror, then ha, ha) and line 1. Plain, a little funny, and it adds to 'use the fear' without repeating it. It fits the Judgment page. Glad to post.

history.text:
Two mountains:
think no further.
history.why: Mountain on mountain is stillness doubled, and the Image says not to think beyond where you are.
history.feedback:
True to the Image, but it repeats the short: the hook is 'Can't stop overthinking?' and the meaning is 'Stay with where you are now.' 'Think no further' says the same thing again in slightly stiff wording. Use a line that adds something concrete. Line 5: 'Still your jaw:
your words make sense.' is too long, so try 'Still jaw,
words in order.' Or line 1, 'Stop it at
the toes.' (catch the impulse before it moves). As a line lesson it also breaks up the run of 'lines' kinds.

history.text:
Out of place? Find
a flat branch.
history.why: A goose in a tree, where geese don't belong, finds a flat branch; no fault.
history.feedback: True, but the goose, the thing that makes the line funny and clear, is missing. Without it, 'find a flat branch' is cryptic, like the rejected watchtower lesson, and the lit-line picture shows no goose to fill in the gap. Put the goose in: 'A goose in a tree:\nfind a flat branch.' (18/18).

history.text:
The princess wore
the plainer dress.
history.why: The emperor's daughter dressed plainer than her attendant, and it resolves well.
history.feedback: True to line 5: the princess's sleeves were plainer than her attendant's, and it resolves well. Concrete and surprising, in the same vein as the approved 'guest, not inspector.' It adds to the short rather than repeating it. Glad to post.

history.text:
Time to settle
disputes.
history.why: Thunder and lightning arrive together, force with clarity, so the Image says: decide the cases.
history.feedback: True to the Image, but abstract, and it says nothing about the two trigrams the picture shows. It also repeats the question ('What will you decide now?'). No viewer would send it to a friend. Switch to line 6, which is concrete and surprising: 'The biggest house,\nand no one home.' (17/15). Or line 2/4, 'So many screens,\nstars at noon.' 54 and 56 are both line, so if you go to line kind, move one neighbour off line, or keep 55 as lines with a sentence that names thunder and lightning.

history.text:
The wanderer burns
his own inn.
history.why: A guest who wrecks the shelter he was given loses his helper too.
history.feedback: True to line 3. Concrete, a little funny, and it gives the consequence of 'You're a guest. Act like one.' without repeating it. One small point: 'own' is not quite right, because the inn is not his, and the synthesis makes that the point. 'The wanderer burns\ndown the inn.' is more exact.

history.text:
No beginning,
but an end.
history.why: Gentle change is so gradual you can't say when it started, only when it finished.
history.feedback: True to line 5, but it is cryptic in the same way as the rejected watchtower lesson. A viewer reading it for two seconds learns nothing. It needs the subject: 'Change you can't\ndate, but it ends.' Or pick a more concrete line: line 3 (repeating the same thing again and again brings friction, which is a nice turn against 'say it again'), or line 2, 'Something under\nthe bed? Call help.'

history.text:
Joy with friends:
talk and practice.
history.why: Kroyer's toast at Skagen shows the Image: friends joined for discussion and practice.
history.feedback: True to the Image, and the Krøyer toast works at a glance, like the approved Renoir. But 'Joy with friends' largely repeats the meaning ('share it') and the painting's own point, and 'practice' is vague: practice what? Try 'Friends who talk\nand learn together' (16/18), which renders 'discussion and practice' (講習, study together) more clearly.

history.text:
Break up your own
group: very good.
history.why: The line's surprise: dissolving your own group supremely resolves well.
history.feedback: True to line 4 and properly surprising. But against the hook 'People drifting apart?', 'Break up your own group' can read as advice to break up with your friends. 'very good' is also flat. Say what the break gains: 'Drop your faction,\ngain the whole.' (17/15). That is closer to 'dispersion creates accumulation.'

history.text:
A lake holds only
so much water.
history.why: Water over the lake: knowing your capacity is what keeps you from flooding.
history.feedback: True to the Image, and it fits the trigrams picture (water above the lake) directly. Plain and concrete. It stays close to 'Where's your limit?' but gives the reason in a picture, so it still adds something. Glad to post.

history.text:
Truth even reaches
pigs and fish.
history.why: The Judgment opens with piglets and fish: real sincerity reaches even them.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment and its synthesis. Concrete, funny, and it answers the hook 'Can't get through to someone?' well. 'Truth' instead of 'sincerity' is close enough. Glad to post.

history.text:
Extra polite,
extra frugal.
history.why: The Image allows excess only downward: more reverence, more grief, more frugality.
history.feedback: Mostly true. The Image says to exceed in reverence, grief and frugality, and 'polite' understates reverence. It is abstract, and it does not connect to the thunder-on-mountain picture. Line 2 is concrete and funny: 'Missed the king?\nSee the minister.' (15/16). The neighbours become judgment, line, line, judgment, which is allowed. If you keep lines, name the images, e.g. 'Thunder, small\non a mountain' plus the point.

history.text:
Fine silk turns
to rags.
history.why: After completion, decay is slow and quiet, so the line says to stay watchful all day.
history.feedback: True to line 4. A concrete picture of slow decay that adds to 'stay alert' without repeating it. Glad to post. If there were room it could hint at 'watch all day,' but it works as it is.

history.text:
The little fox
wets its tail.
history.why: The book ends on a fox that almost crossed the river: not yet.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment, and a good last line for the series. But it drops 'almost crossed', which is the whole point, so a viewer who does not know the story sees only a fox with a wet tail. It also echoes 63's line 1 image. Add the 'almost': 'Almost across,\nthe fox gets wet.' (14/16) or 'Almost across:\nthe fox's wet tail.' (14/18).

history.text:
Some change deep.
Some, just faces.
history.why: The realized person changes like a leopard; petty people change only their faces: same person, new face.
history.feedback: True to line 6 ('The realized person transforms like a leopard. The petty change only their faces.') and it adds something the short doesn't say. Two problems. 'Some change deep' is awkward English ('deeply'). It also drops the leopard, the one concrete image, so the first half says nothing specific. Use the book's own words: "The petty change\nonly their faces." (16/17 chars, 6 words). Or keep the contrast: "A leopard changes.\nOthers swap faces." (17/17).

history.text:
The legs break.
The duke wears it.
history.why: The caldron's legs break and the duke's meal spills over him: a vessel not set right fails on the person it serves.
history.feedback: True to line 4 (legs break, the duke's meal overturned, his person soiled). It is concrete and a little funny, and it shows what happens if you don't 'set it right', so it ends the short well. The weak spot is 'wears it': nothing on screen says what 'it' is. The picture is a lit line, not a pot, so a viewer needs the word dinner or meal. Try "The legs break.\nDuke wears dinner." (15/17) or "The pot tips over.\nDuke wears dinner." Also check neighbours: 49 and 50 are both line lessons, so 51 must not be a line.

history.text:
Give your thoughts
a boundary.
history.why: Mountain beside mountain: stillness comes not by emptying the mind but by giving it a boundary.
history.feedback: The source is the commentary's synthesis ('by giving it a boundary'), not the book. The book's Image says only 'thinks of nothing beyond their present situation', which is almost word for word the short's meaning ('Stay with where you are now'), so this repeats the short. It is also abstract, and a plain command to the viewer, not a picture. Two mountains don't clearly say 'boundary' at a glance. Better: switch to a line. Line 5 is concrete and surprising: 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.' Try "Still the jaw,\nwords find order." (14/16). Or use the Judgment: 'Walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people.'

history.text:
Goose in a tree:
a flat branch.
history.why: A wild goose is out of place in a tree, and the line's advice is to find a flat branch to stand on.
history.feedback: True to line 4 and the best kind of material: a goose in a tree is concrete and a little funny. But the lesson is the advice, and without a verb 'a flat branch' reads like a caption, not a point. Add the verb: "Goose in a tree?\nFind a flat branch." (16/18). It moves away from the short's step-by-step theme, which is fine because it adds something new.

history.text:
Thunder to act,
lightning to see.
history.why: Thunder and lightning arrive together: force and clarity at the same time, the moment to judge.
history.feedback: It fits the trigram picture (thunder over fire/lightning). But act/see is the commentary's split. The book says 'decides disputes and carries out punishments', and the short's question already asks 'What will you decide now?'. The parallel phrasing is a little mannered and abstract, and nobody would send it to a friend. Better: lines 2/4 have the book's most surprising image, 'So abundant are the screens that the Big Dipper is visible at midday'. It also ties back to the 'sun at noon' in the meaning. Try "Screens so thick,\nstars at noon." (15/13) as a line lesson.

history.text:
Say it too often:
friction.
history.why: Repeated penetration brings friction: repeating past the point of use becomes its own obstruction.
history.feedback: Line 3 is 'Repeated penetration. Friction.' Reading it as speech is a stretch, but the Image ('reiterates commands') supports it. It is a nice turn against the short's 'say it again'. The problem is the ending: a colon plus the single word 'friction' is cryptic, and 'friction' is abstract for a two-second read. Say what happens in plain words: "Said too often,\nit grates." (15/9), or "Say it again,\nnot ten times." if the writer wants to keep the contrast with the meaning.

history.text:
Talk and learn
with friends.
history.why: Joined lakes: the realized person joins with friends for discussion and practice, and Krøyer's toast shows it.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('joins with friends for discussion and practice'), but it mostly repeats the short: the hook is 'no one to tell' and the meaning is 'share it'. The painting shows a toast, not talking and learning, so the words and the picture don't match. The line is flat. Either keep the painting and write a sentence that fits the toast, or switch to a line with an edge: line 4 ('Deliberated joy is not yet at peace. Setting aside the urgency brings happiness') or line 3 ('Approaching joy. Adverse'), e.g. "Chasing joy\ngoes wrong." Hexagrams 57 to 59 are line/painting/line, so the variety rule is fine either way.

history.text:
Drop your faction,
gain the whole.
history.why: Dispersing one's own group resolves supremely well: dispersion creates accumulation beyond any faction.
history.feedback: The line text supports it ('Dispersing one's group. Supremely resolves well. Dispersion creates accumulation'), and it is the counterintuitive kind of point that makes people rewatch. It adds to the hook ('People drifting apart?') without repeating it. 'Gain the whole' is the commentary's abstraction, and 'faction' is a bit formal. Plainer: "Break up your side,\nmore gathers." or "Drop your clique,\ngain everyone." (16/14).

history.text:
Missed the king?
See the minister.
history.why: Not reaching the ruler, meeting the minister: in a small time the tier below is the right channel, no fault.
history.feedback: True to line 2 ('Not reaching the ruler, meeting the minister. No fault'). It is concrete, plain, a little funny, and it fits the short's 'small' theme without repeating the hook, meaning or question. Glad to post. Keep an eye on variety with 60, 61 and 63.

history.text:
Almost across,
the fox gets wet.
history.why: The little fox has almost crossed and wets its tail: the last step is where it goes wrong.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment: the fox is the best-known image in the book and a fitting last word for the series. 'Almost across' echoes the hook ('So close to done?') a little, but the fox makes it a new thing. One small fix for precision: the book says the tail gets wet, and that detail is the joke. Try "Almost across,\nfox wets its tail." (14/18).

history.text:
The petty change
only their faces.
history.why: The realized person changes like a leopard, all through; the petty change only the face they show.
history.feedback: True: line 6 reads 'The realized person transforms like a leopard. The petty change only their faces.' It fits the lit line and adds something the short doesn't say (surface change versus real change). The problem is 'The petty' used as a noun. People don't talk that way, so the viewer stops to parse it. It also gives only half the contrast: the leopard, the concrete and surprising half, is cut. A better version keeps the leopard, e.g. 'Leopards change\nall through.' If you keep the petty half, make it plain: 'Some change only\ntheir faces.'

history.text:
The legs break.
Duke wears dinner.
history.why: The caldron's legs break, the duke's meal spills over him: what happens when the setup isn't right.
history.feedback: True to line 4: legs break, the duke's meal overturned, his person soiled. It is concrete and funny, and it pays off the short's 'get set up before you start' by showing what happens when you don't. I would post it. The only flaw is that 'Duke wears dinner' reads like a headline. 'The duke wears\nhis dinner.' is slightly plainer if the line limits allow.

history.text:
In the courtyard,
see no one.
history.why: Walking through the courtyard without seeing the people: still enough inside that the crowd doesn't pull at you.
history.feedback: True to the Judgment ('walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people'), but it is too cryptic, the same problem as the rejected watchtower. Without the synthesis, 'see no one' reads as avoiding people or loneliness, not inner stillness. It also adds little to 'What can wait?'. Better: line 5, 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.', e.g. 'Still the jaw,\nwords find order.' (concrete and useful). Or line 1, which starts the body-part climb: 'Stillness starts\nat the toes.'

history.text:
Goose in a tree?
Find flat footing.
history.why: A goose can't grip a branch; in the wrong place it looks for a flat perch, and there is no fault.
history.feedback: True to line 4: the goose advances to the trees and perhaps finds a flat branch, no fault. It is concrete, a little funny, a good fit for the lit line, and it adds a new angle (being in the wrong place) to 'step by step'. One fix: 'flat footing' is alliteration the text doesn't have. The text's own 'a flat branch' is more concrete and fits in 18 characters: 'Goose in a tree?\nFind a flat branch.'

history.text:
Don't spend noon
fearing sunset.
history.why: The sun at midday is about to descend; the Judgment says not to worry, because worrying about the afternoon wastes the noon.
history.feedback: The synthesis supports it (worrying about the afternoon wastes the noon), but it repeats the short's own meaning lines ('Abundance says: don't worry' / 'Be the sun at noon') almost word for word, so it adds nothing after the question. 'Sunset' is also a picture the book doesn't use. Change kind and content. Line 6 is concrete and surprising: 'So abundant his dwelling... peering through the gate, no one there. For three years, seeing no one.' For example: 'A huge house,\nand no one home.' Lines 2 and 4 also have the odd 'Big Dipper visible at midday' image.

history.text:
Said too often,
it grates.
history.why: Repeated penetration brings friction: say it again, but past a point repetition wears people down.
history.feedback: Line 3 reads 'Repeated penetration. Friction.' The Image's 'reiterates commands' supports reading it as speech. It works as a turn: the short says 'say it again', and this lesson sets the limit, which adds something real. It is plain. It is a little abstract for the lit-line picture, and the app's synthesis reads line 3 as overthinking, not nagging, so it is a slight stretch of the commentary. It would reach 8 if it named the listener, e.g. 'Say it too often,\nit grates.', which makes the link to the short's advice explicit.

history.text:
Painters toast,
then talk shop.
history.why: Krøyer's artists at their party: the Image joins friends for discussion and practice, not only celebration.
history.feedback: True to the Image: 'joins with friends for discussion and practice.' 'Talk shop' is a plain, funny way to say discussion and practice. 'Painters' matches the Krøyer artists' party on screen, and it adds to 'share it' by saying joy with friends includes working together. One small gap: the canvas shows the toast, not the shop talk, so the second half comes from the text, not the picture. That is acceptable at a glance. Glad to post.

history.text:
Leave your clique,
more will gather.
history.why: Dispersing one's own group resolves well: breaking up the faction gathers more people, against ordinary expectation.
history.feedback: True to line 4: 'Dispersing one's group. Supremely resolves well. Dispersion creates accumulation.' It is surprising and plain, and it fits the short's theme of people drifting apart. The problem is 'Leave': the line means dissolving your own faction, not walking away from it, and 'leave your clique, more will gather' can read as 'go find new friends'. Better: 'End your clique,\nmore will gather.' or 'Drop your faction,\nmore will gather.'

history.text:
Some change only
their faces.
history.why: The realized person changes like a leopard; the petty change only their faces, so surface change is not the real thing.
history.feedback: True: line 6 says 'The petty change only their faces.' The lesson adds to the short, whose copy is about waiting and trust, and it is a little wry. The problem is that the line sets the petty against the leopard, and the lesson drops the leopard, so it reads as half a sentence. A viewer gets 'some people fake it' but not the point that real change goes deeper. Better to keep the contrast in plain words, e.g. 'Real change goes\npast the face.' Or use line 3, which is concrete and surprising: 'Wait till it's said\nthree times.' That fits 18 characters per line, and the line says trust comes once talk of the change has gone around three times. Check it does not echo the meaning line 'Trust comes on the last day' too closely.

history.text:
Still inside,
while you walk.
history.why: The Judgment walks through the courtyard: stillness is not freezing in place, it is keeping still inside while you keep moving.
history.feedback: Close to the Judgment synthesis ('You're walking. You just stopped grasping'), but 'Still inside' is the synthesis's gloss. The Judgment itself says 'stilling the back… walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people.' The phrasing is clipped and a bit cryptic, and it sits near the short's own 'pause / stay with where you are now.' Nothing concrete to remember or send to a friend. Better: line 5, 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order.' → 'Still your jaw,\nyour words make sense.' (15/19, so trim: 'Still your jaw,\nwords make sense.'). It is concrete, a little funny, true to the line, and answers the 'overthinking' hook. Or use the Hokusai Red Fuji painting the input offers, if painting fits the variety count here.

history.text:
Lightning to see,
thunder to act.
history.why: Thunder over fire: abundance gives clear sight and the force to act at the same time, and that window does not last.
history.feedback: True to the Image ('Thunder and lightning both arrive') and its synthesis (clarity to see, force to act). The parallel is neat and plain. Two problems. The picture labels the lower trigram FIRE 火, not lightning, so the viewer has to make that jump in two seconds. 'Thunder to act' also leans on the short's own question 'What will you decide now?' instead of adding something new. It is also abstract rather than surprising. Stronger: line 2/4, 'So abundant are the screens that the Big Dipper is visible at midday' → 'So dark at noon\nyou see stars.' It is concrete and odd, and it adds the warning side of abundance after 'be the sun at noon.' Line 4 ends with meeting the hidden master in the dark, which makes it the kinder choice. If you keep the lines kind, match the label: 'Fire to see,\nthunder to act.'

history.text:
Say it too often,
it grates.
history.why: Line 3, repeated penetration brings friction: repeating has a limit, past which the listener pushes back.
history.feedback: Line 3 says 'Repeated penetration. Friction.' Reading it as speech is fair given the Image's 'reiterates commands', though the app's synthesis reads the line as overthinking. It works well against the short. The copy says 'say it again' and asks 'What's worth repeating today?', and this answers with the limit. It is plain, a little funny, and something you would send to a friend. Keep it. One small option: 'Say it too often,\nit starts to grate.' reads more like speech, but it is 19 characters on line 2, so the current version is fine.

history.text:
Drop your faction,
more will gather.
history.why: Dissolving your own group supremely resolves well: dispersion creates accumulation, more than any faction could hold.
history.feedback: True to line 4: 'Dispersing one's group. Supremely resolves well. Dispersion creates accumulation.' It is counterintuitive and adds to a short whose copy is about reminding people of a shared origin. It lands at a glance. 'Faction' is slightly formal; 'Drop your own side,\nmore will gather.' is plainer if you want it. Otherwise glad to post.

history.text:
Fire in a lake:
set the calendar.
history.why: Fire within the lake, and the response is to organize the calendar: a revolution is naming that one season ended and another began.
history.feedback: The Image does say this: 'Fire within the lake ... organizes the calendar and clarifies the seasons.' Mechanically it passes: 7 words, lines of 15 and 17 characters. It fits the LAKE over FIRE picture and does not repeat the copy ('finish first', 'trust comes on the last day'). The problem is that it does not land. A new viewer cannot see in two seconds why a revolution means setting a calendar, because the link ('one season ended, name it') is only in the synthesis. This is close to the rejected 'Its shape: a watchtower.' Better: line 6, 'The petty change / only their faces.' (lines of 16 and 15 characters), with LINE 6 lit. It is concrete, a little funny, true to the text ('The petty change only their faces'), and it adds to the short's point about real change. If it stays a lines lesson, spell the link out, e.g. 'A new season: / say so, mark it.' The line 6 lesson is stronger.

history.text:
Cross the yard,
see no one.
history.why: The Judgment: walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people, no fault; you keep moving but nothing around you grabs you.
history.feedback: The Judgment says 'Walking through the courtyard, not seeing the people. No fault.' Mechanically it passes: 6 words, lines of 15 and 11 characters. The trouble is the wording. 'See no one' reads as an empty yard or as ignoring people. The text means the people are there and they do not pull you in. Read cold, it sounds lonely or rude, not still. It also echoes 55 line 6 ('seeing no one', adverse), which runs near it in the series. Better: line 5, 'Still your jaw: / words come in order.' Trim it to fit 18 characters, e.g. 'Still the jaw, / words line up.' It is concrete, a little funny, true to 'Stilling the jaws. Words have order,' and it fits a hook about overthinking. Line 1 also works: 'Stop it / at the toes.' If you keep the Judgment, rephrase to keep the people in: 'Walk past people, / don't get pulled.'

history.text:
Fire to see,
thunder to act.
history.why: Thunder over fire: the clarity to see and the force to act arrive together in abundance, and that window is when you judge.
history.feedback: It is true to the Image synthesis (lightning is clarity, thunder is force), and it fits the THUNDER over FIRE picture. Mechanically it passes: 6 words, lines of 12 and 15 characters. But it is abstract and reads like a slogan: the balanced 'X to see, Y to act' pattern is the mannered style the rules ban. A viewer learns nothing concrete. It also leans on the question 'What will you decide now?' without adding to it. The Image's actual point, judging disputes, is left out. Better: line 6, 'Biggest house, / no one home.' (lines of 14 and 12 characters), with LINE 6 lit. It is concrete, true to 'So abundant his dwelling ... desolate, no one there. For three years, seeing no one,' and it gives a short about 'at your peak, don't worry' a sharp ending. Line 2 or 4 is another option: 'Stars at noon: / the screens too thick.' (check the length).
